We investigated the trophic consequences of coastal acidification for Solitary Sandpipers (*Tringa solitaria*) across 15 migration stopover sites in the Gulf of Mexico from 2018-2022. Using pH loggers and benthic sampling, we documented a 0.3-0.5 unit decline in estuarine water pH during peak migration months (April-May, September-October), correlating with atmospheric CO₂ increases (r = -0.72, p<0.001). Stomach content analysis (n=127 individuals) revealed acidified sites had 42% lower abundance of calcium-rich prey (amphipods, gastropods; χ²=15.3, p=0.004), forcing shifts to softer-bodied chironomid larvae (65% diet proportion vs. 28% at control sites). Captive feeding trials demonstrated calcium-deficient diets reduced juvenile bone density by 14% (micro-CT scan analysis; t=3.11, p=0.02) and flight muscle mass by 19% (ANOVA F=8.7, p=0.006). However, geolocator data (n=45 adults) showed no significant difference in migration speed between acidification-exposed and control groups (Mann-Whitney U=212, p=0.34), suggesting behavioral compensation through extended foraging times. Population models incorporating acidification projections indicate a 23% decline in first-year survival by 2050 under RCP8.5 scenarios, primarily driven by calcium limitation during post-fledging development. These findings highlight previously understudied indirect pathways through which ocean acidification threatens shorebirds, emphasizing the need for watershed-scale management of carbonate chemistry in critical stopover habitats.

We investigated how changing cyclonic patterns in the North Atlantic influence foraging ecology and stopover duration of Curlew Sandpipers (Calidris ferruginea) at the Banc d'Arguin, Mauritania, with particular focus on interactions between storm-mediated habitat changes and invasive smooth cordgrass (Spartina alterniflora). Using GPS tracking (n=48 individuals) coupled with monthly vegetation surveys (2015-2022), we quantified shorebird responses to 37 documented storm events affecting this critical West African wintering site. Mixed-effects models revealed storm frequency increased 42% (p=0.013) over the study period, correlating with 19% expansion of Spartina (R²=0.71). While curlews showed 23% higher prey intake rates (95% CI: 15-31%) in Spartina-invaded areas during post-storm periods, these gains were offset by 15% longer invertebrate handling times (p=0.042) and 31% higher thermoregulatory costs measured via doubly-labeled water (n=127 blood samples). Juveniles exhibited 17% lower mass gain rates than adults in invaded habitats (t=2.89, p=0.004), suggesting age-specific vulnerability to habitat transformation. Counterintuitively, satellite telemetry showed curlews increased stopover duration by 5.2 days (SE±1.1) following storms with Spartina presence, likely compensating for reduced foraging efficiency. Our results demonstrate how invasive species mediate shorebird responses to climate-driven disturbance regimes, with critical implications for dynamic habitat management in rapidly changing coastal ecosystems.

We investigated the impacts of sea level rise on American Avocet (Recurvirostra americana) breeding habitats along the Gulf Coast from 2010-2020, analyzing 35 coastal sites across Texas and Louisiana. Using a combination of satellite tracking (n=120 adults with GPS loggers), nest monitoring (2,347 nests), and habitat modeling, we quantified changes in preferred hypersaline flat habitats. Landsat-derived NDVI and NOAA tidal data revealed a 35% reduction in optimal breeding areas (elevation 0.2-0.6m above mean sea level) coinciding with a 14cm local sea level rise (r= -0.78, p<0.001). Nest success declined by 22% in fragmented habitats compared to contiguous areas (logistic exposure daily survival rate: 0.972 vs 0.985, p=0.003), with flooding accounting for 68% of documented failures. Bayesian survival analysis showed strong site fidelity despite habitat degradation (median return rate=0.81), creating ecological traps in seven previously productive zones. However, 23% of tracked individuals shifted to novel inland impoundments, where early-season nests showed equivalent success rates to traditional sites (χ²=1.34, p=0.247). Projections using IPCC RCP 8.5 scenarios indicate 89% loss of current nesting habitat by 2050, but identify 1,200ha of emerging secondary salt flats at higher elevations. Our results emphasize the need for dynamic habitat management strategies that accommodate both avocet adaptability and accelerating coastal squeeze, prioritizing protection of transitional zones with natural sedimentation processes.

We investigated the effects of commercial shell collection on Long-billed Dowitcher (Limnodromus scolopaceus) molt migration in the Fraser River Delta, British Columbia, using a combination of radio telemetry (n=48 adults, 2019-2021) and benthic invertebrate sampling. Molting individuals showed strong site fidelity to intertidal zones with high densities of Hydrobia ulvae (mean 4,112 ± 329 individuals/m²), their primary prey during feather replacement. However, sites subjected to monthly commercial shell harvesting (targeting Mya arenaria) exhibited 30.4% lower H. ulvae biomass (ANOVA: F₁,₂₂=8.71, p=0.007) and 15-day longer molt durations (Kaplan-Meier log-rank test: χ²=6.32, p=0.012) compared to protected areas. A before-after-control-impact analysis revealed that experimentally harvested plots showed 63% reduction in dowitcher foraging density within 72 hours (GLMM: β=-1.42 ± 0.31, z=-4.58, p<0.001). Plasma metabolite profiling indicated elevated corticosterone (mean 18.7 ng/ml vs. 12.3 ng/ml in controls) and reduced triglyceride levels in birds using harvested areas, suggesting physiological stress. Survival analysis revealed 14% lower overwinter survival probabilities for individuals delayed in molt completion (Cox PH model: HR=1.72, 95% CI 1.12-2.64). Our results demonstrate that shell extraction disrupts critical resource landscapes during this vulnerable life stage, with cascading effects on migratory timing and individual fitness. We propose temporal harvest closures during peak molt periods (August-October) to buffer these impacts on declining L. scolopaceus populations along the Pacific Flyway.

We examined the behavioral responses of Mountain Plovers (Charadrius montanus) to experimental egg collection through a controlled field study in Colorado's shortgrass prairie during the 2022 breeding season (May-July). Thirty-two nesting adults (16 pairs) were randomly assigned to control (n=8) or egg removal treatments simulating conservation collection protocols (1 egg removed daily until clutch completion). Foraging behavior was quantified using 10-minute focal observations paired with GPS-accelerometer loggers (n=1,256 observation bouts). Removal treatment birds showed 28% greater daily foraging time compared to controls (F₁,₂₈=5.37, p=0.028), with significantly higher movement rates between foraging patches (2.3±0.4 vs 1.7±0.3 relocations/hr; t=3.12, p=0.004). Peck rates declined 15% in removal groups during early incubation (χ²=8.42, p=0.015), indicating reduced foraging efficiency. Multivariate analysis revealed distinct behavioral syndromes between treatments (PERMANOVA F₁,₃₀=6.89, p=0.002), driven by time budget re-allocation toward vigilance behaviors. Despite these shifts, body condition indices showed no significant differences between groups (t=0.92, p=0.367), suggesting compensatory mechanisms. Our results demonstrate that Mountain Plovers exhibit flexible behavioral responses to egg collection pressure, maintaining energy balance through increased foraging effort at potential costs to nest protection and self-maintenance. These findings support staggered collection timing to allow recovery periods and inform adaptive management strategies for sustainable harvest in conservation breeding programs.

Coastal modification through shoreline armoring presents critical challenges for ground-nesting shorebirds, yet species-specific responses remain poorly quantified. We investigated habitat selection and behavioral adaptations of Pied Avocets (n = 45 adults) along 120 km of armored versus natural shorelines in the Wadden Sea (2019-2022 breeding seasons) using GPS telemetry (5-minute fix intervals) and systematic habitat surveys. Resource selection functions revealed strong avoidance of armored segments (β = -1.73, SE = 0.41, p < 0.001), with a 72% reduction in foraging probability within 50 m of revetments compared to natural sediments. Generalized linear mixed models showed nesting density declined by 63% (95% CI: 51-72%) along armored shores despite comparable prey biomass (ANOVA F1,118 = 1.92, p = 0.17). Behavioral observations (n = 340 hours) documented 34% higher vigilance rates (t = 4.12, df = 337, p < 0.001) and 18% lower prey intake rates (Wilcoxon V = 2810, p = 0.003) at armored sites. However, 21% of tracked individuals showed partial adaptation through nocturnal foraging peaks (22:00-04:00) in lower-intertidal zones unaffected by daytime tourist activity. Our multi-year analysis reveals shoreline armoring disproportionately impacts breeding avocets through cascading effects on habitat availability and foraging efficiency, though individual behavioral plasticity may mitigate some energetic costs. These findings underscore the need for managed coastal realignment strategies that maintain tidal flat connectivity while addressing synergetic pressures from recreational disturbance.

We investigated the effects of recreational kite flying on Surfbird (Calidris virgata) foraging behavior along the Pacific coast of Alaska's Kenai Peninsula during spring migration (April-May 2021-2023). Using focal animal sampling (n=228 individuals) and controlled disturbance experiments across 12 intertidal sites (6 kite-flying zones, 6 controls), we quantified foraging rates, vigilance behavior, and prey intake before, during, and after kite exposure. Mixed-effects models revealed kite presence reduced surfbird foraging efficiency by 27% (β=-0.31, SE=0.07, p<0.001), with individuals increasing vigilance time from 12% to 42% of observational intervals (Wald χ²=34.7, p<0.0001). Foraging site fidelity decreased by 18% in experimental zones compared to controls following repeated kite disturbances (F₁,₁₁₈=9.2, p=0.003). However, prey sampling (n=452 core samples) showed no significant differences in polychaete worm biomass between disturbed and control areas (t=1.41, p=0.16), suggesting behavioral responses rather than prey depletion drove observed changes. Wind speed mediated effects, with critical thresholds for behavioral responses occurring at ≥8 m/s (AUC=0.79), when kites remained consistently airborne. Our results demonstrate that ephemeral anthropogenic disturbances can disproportionately impact energy acquisition in staging shorebirds, particularly under marginal foraging conditions. These findings underscore the need for targeted management of recreational activities in intertidal habitats during peak migration periods when surfbirds require maximal daily energy intake (mean 12.3 kJ/hr) to fuel northward migrations.

We investigated relationships between parasitic infections and trophic ecology in breeding Piping Plovers (Charadrius melodus) along the U.S. Atlantic Coast using stable isotope analysis (δ15N, δ13C) and parasitological surveys. From 2018-2020, 152 adults and 87 juveniles were sampled across 12 breeding sites from Virginia to Maine. Fecal samples revealed trematode (Microphallus spp.) and nematode (Capillaria spp.) infections in 43% of adults and 62% of juveniles. Isotope values from rectrix feathers and blood plasma showed infected individuals exhibited significantly higher δ15N values (+1.3‰, p=0.012) compared to uninfected conspecifics, suggesting increased consumption of higher-trophic-level prey in intertidal zones (η²=0.35). However, no isotopic differences were detected between infection status in juveniles (p=0.41). Adults with trematode infections showed reduced body condition indices (scaled mass index = -2.1, p=0.047) despite similar foraging signatures, while infected juveniles displayed no such effects. Multivariate models indicated infection likelihood increased with proximity to rocky substrates (OR=3.2, 95% CI:1.4-7.1) and amphipod-dominated diets (δ13C > -14‰; OR=2.7). Our results demonstrate life stage-specific interactions between parasitism and foraging ecology, with adult plovers potentially facing energetic trade-offs from infection that are absent in juveniles. These findings highlight the need for habitat management strategies that consider invertebrate prey community composition as a determinant of parasite exposure in this threatened shorebird species.

We investigated the impacts of recreational shell collection on Common Ringed Plover (Charadrius hiaticula) stopover ecology in the German Wadden Sea (53°54′N, 8°33′E) during 2019-2021 spring migrations. Using a paired design comparing 6 shell-rich beaches with active collection to 6 control sites, we tracked 45 GPS-tagged adults and conducted 1,235 behavioral scans. Shell-collected sites showed 32% lower plover densities (GLMM: β = -1.15 ± 0.23 SE, p = 0.02) and 41% reduced foraging time budgets. Prey availability assessments revealed 40% fewer polychaetes (Hediste diversicolor) in collection areas (t-test: t = 3.89, df=10, p=0.003), correlating with reduced plover intake rates (r = 0.78, p<0.001). Telemetry data indicated 19% shorter stopover durations (median 2.3 vs 2.8 days) at impacted sites, though survival probabilities (0.92 ± 0.04 SE) showed no significant difference. Surprisingly, 68% of tracked individuals exhibited compensatory feeding by utilizing adjacent mussel beds during low tide, potentially mitigating energetic deficits. Our mark-recapture models suggest cumulative exposure effects, with repeat migrants showing 12% higher site fidelity to undisturbed areas (χ² = 5.67, p=0.017). These findings highlight the sensitivity of stopover site selection to anthropogenic substrate alteration, particularly given the 34% increase in shell collection permits issued since 2015. While plovers demonstrate behavioral flexibility, sustained shell removal may erode the carrying capacity of key staging habitats, emphasizing the need for seasonal collection bans during peak migration periods.

We investigated nest trampling risks for Black-tailed Godwits (Limosa limosa) in the Netherlands' agricultural grasslands using GPS telemetry (n=42 adults tracked across 15 sites during 2020-2023 breeding seasons). High-resolution movement data (5-minute intervals) revealed cattle preferentially used 63% of nest-containing parcels, with 18% of monitored nests (n=127) failing due to trampling as verified by trail cameras. Nest survival analysis showed trampling probability increased 2.3-fold (95% CI: 1.7-3.1) in fields with stocking densities >1.5 livestock units/ha, though trampling accounted for only 14% of total nest losses compared to 58% from predation. Adults nesting in intensively grazed pastures (≤30 cm vegetation) exhibited 37% shorter incubation bout durations (mean=43±11 min vs. 68±15 min in taller swards; p<0.001) and 2.1× higher abandonment rates. Contrary to expectations, tracked cattle spent <8% of time within 5 m of nests, with trampling risk peaking at dawn/dusk when godwit nest relief coincided with livestock movement (χ²=9.4, p=0.002). Spatial models identified floodplain meadows as lower-risk habitats compared to drained polders (AUC=0.78). Our results suggest targeted grazing restrictions during peak incubation (days 15-21) could reduce trampling mortality by 41% without major agricultural impacts, though habitat quality mediates site-specific vulnerability. This study demonstrates how integrating telemetry across species enhances understanding of human-wildlife conflict mechanisms in shared landscapes.

We investigated the effects of recreational disturbance on energy budgets of American Golden-Plovers (Pluvialis dominica) during spring migration in the Central Flyway (Nebraska, USA; 2019-2022). Using heart rate telemetry (n=35 adults) and plasma metabolite analysis, we quantified daily energy expenditure (DEE) across 12 stopover sites with varying human activity levels. Plovers in high-disturbance areas (>15 recreational events/day within 200 m) exhibited 23% higher DEE (mean ± SE: 145.3 ± 4.7 kJ/day) compared to low-disturbance sites (118.1 ± 3.2 kJ/day; linear mixed-effects model: β=0.41, p<0.001). Increased vigilance behavior (35% more scan bouts/hour) and frequent flight responses to pedestrians (mean flight initiation distance=42 m) accounted for 68% of the energy differential. However, individuals demonstrating <5% DEE increase (n=7) showed significantly shorter inter-flush intervals (ρ=-0.63, p=0.02), suggesting partial habituation. Fat deposition rates in disturbed areas averaged 0.21 g/day versus 0.47 g/day in protected zones (Mann-Whitney U=112, p=0.004), potentially delaying migration readiness by 3-5 days. Our results indicate non-lethal disturbances impose substantial energetic costs, though individual variation in response strategies may buffer population-level impacts. These findings support implementing seasonal recreation restrictions within 300 m of key stopover wetlands during peak migration periods (April 15-May 10).

Recent range contraction in Red Phalaropes (Phalaropus fulicarius) within oil-impacted regions of the Arctic has raised concerns about genetic vulnerability to environmental stressors. We analyzed genomic diversity (ddRADseq) in 247 individuals across six breeding colonies (Beaufort Sea, Hudson Bay, North Atlantic) and three wintering areas (Peruvian Upwelling, Benguela Current) to assess population structure and selection signals related to hydrocarbon exposure. Microsatellite analysis (15 loci) revealed significantly reduced heterozygosity (HE = 0.58 vs. 0.72, p < 0.001) and effective population size (Ne = 312 vs. 892) in Beaufort Sea breeders compared to other colonies, coinciding with chronic oiling events from 2010-2020. FST analysis (global FST = 0.083) showed moderate differentiation between Pacific and Atlantic flyways but panmixia within ocean basins. Unexpectedly, four candidate genomic regions under selection contained genes linked to cytochrome P450 detoxification pathways (CYP2AH1, CYP3A7), though allele frequencies showed no spatial correlation with oil spill histories (Mantel test r = 0.12, p = 0.34). Telomere length analysis (qPCR) revealed 23% shorter telomeres in oil-exposed juveniles (n = 47) versus controls (n = 53, p = 0.012), suggesting sublethal physiological impacts. Our results indicate that localized population declines in heavily oiled areas may reduce adaptive potential despite high connectivity, underscoring the need for genetic monitoring in environmental risk assessments. Conservation priorities should focus on protecting Beaufort Sea molting habitats while addressing synergistic effects of oil pollution and Arctic warming.

We investigated the relationship between shell collection by humans and parental care strategies in Pied Avocets (Recurvirostra avosetta) across three breeding seasons (2018-2020) in the Sidi Moussa-Walidia Complex, Morocco. Through 1,200 hours of behavioral observations at 67 nests and shell density surveys across 22 breeding islets, we found shell availability (Mya arenaria fragments) significantly influenced nest site selection (GLMM: β = 0.73 ± 0.18 SE, p < 0.001) and incubation bout duration. Nests with ≥30 shells/m² (n=41) experienced 35% lower predation rates compared to low-shell nests (n=26, χ²=12.4, p=0.002), likely due to improved camouflage. However, experimental shell removal (n=15 nests) revealed compensatory behaviors: parents increased nest attendance by 22% (paired t-test: t=3.81, p=0.002) but showed 18% lower foraging efficiency. Shell collection pressure (estimated at 0.8-1.3 kg/m²/day during low tide) reduced available nesting material by 28% annually, correlating with a 15% decline in hatching success at impacted sites (R²=0.67, p=0.03). GPS tracking of 18 adults demonstrated females compensated for shell scarcity by extending incubation shifts (mean 45 vs. 32 minutes, p=0.017), while males increased territory defense. Our results highlight the non-consumptive impacts of shell harvesting on biparental care systems and suggest habitat management strategies maintaining ≥25 shells/m² could buffer breeding populations against anthropogenic disturbance.

We investigated how human-modified shorelines influence Whimbrel (Numenius phaeopus) behavior and energetics across six coastal sites in the East Atlantic Flyway (Netherlands, Germany, Denmark) during 2020-2022 migration seasons. Using GPS telemetry (n=42 adults), behavioral scans (n=350 disturbance events across 120 observation hours), and GIS-based shoreline change analysis, we quantified responses to armored vs. natural habitats. Individuals in armored zones exhibited 28% higher flight initiation distances (FID) to human approach (mean 42.3 m ± 5.6 SE) compared to natural sites (31.1 m ± 4.2 SE; linear mixed model: β=11.2, p=0.003). Foraging time decreased by 45% in armored habitats due to higher disturbance frequency (3.2 events/hr vs. 1.4 events/hr in natural areas), with energetic models suggesting 18% increased daily intake requirements. Shoreline armoring reduced access to preferred polychaete prey, evidenced by 37% lower intake rates (0.24 prey/min vs. 0.38 prey/min; Mann-Whitney U=412, p<0.001) in armored zones. Despite these impacts, population-level effects appeared muted, with stable site fidelity rates (82% annual return) and no significant decline in local abundance (GLMM: z=1.12, p=0.26). However, first-year survival probabilities decreased 23% at armored stopovers (Cox PH model: HR=1.23, p=0.04). Results suggest Whimbrels exhibit behavioral plasticity to coastal modification but face rising energetic costs that may compromise migration success under intensifying shoreline development. Conservation strategies should prioritize maintaining natural intertidal corridors while testing "soft" armoring designs at critical stopover sites.

We investigated heavy metal contamination and physiological responses of Red Knots (Calidris canutus rufa) to dredging operations in Delaware Bay, USA, during spring migration (2018-2020). Blood samples from 147 individuals and sediment cores from 23 intertidal sites were analyzed for mercury, lead, and cadmium concentrations using ICP-MS. Birds captured near active dredge sites (n=82) showed 37% higher mercury levels (2.8 ± 0.4 ppm vs 2.0 ± 0.3 ppm; p=0.012) and 28% elevated lead concentrations compared to reference areas. Satellite-tagged knots (n=27) exhibited significantly reduced mass gain rates (15.3% decrease; GLMM β = -0.21, SE=0.08) when foraging within 2 km of dredging operations, with plasma metabolite profiling indicating elevated corticosterone (p=0.032) and reduced triglyceride levels (p=0.041). Individuals with blood lead >2.5 ppm demonstrated 18% longer stopover durations (Cox PH hazard ratio=0.62, p=0.047) and 12% lower annual survival rates based on mark-recapture analysis (n=654 banded birds). Sediment metal concentrations exceeded EPA thresholds at 65% of dredge-adjacent sites during operation periods, persisting up to 14 months post-dredging. Juveniles showed greater sensitivity, with 30% higher metal accumulation rates than adults (ANOVA F=8.91, p=0.003). While 42% of tracked birds shifted foraging locations to avoid contaminated zones, habitat compression increased competition at remaining sites. Our results demonstrate cascading effects of dredge-related pollution on shorebird energetics and migration schedules, highlighting the need for temporal management of dredging activities and improved sediment containment measures during critical migration windows.

We investigated the impacts of beach nourishment on Spotted Sandpiper (Actitis macularius) habitat use and foraging ecology along the Delaware Bay shoreline from 2016-2020. Using standardized shorebird surveys (n=412) and GPS tracking of 12 individuals, we compared habitat selection patterns across 8 nourished and 6 natural beach segments. Nourishment projects added an average of 3.2 ± 0.7 m of beach width but reduced intertidal invertebrate biomass by 42% (p=0.02) through sediment compaction and altered grain size composition. Sandpipers exhibited 35% lower foraging rates (1.2 vs. 1.8 prey/min, p<0.01) and 28% shorter residence times (95% CI: 17-39%) at nourished sites compared to natural beaches. Nest monitoring revealed a 63% decline in breeding pair density within nourished zones (0.4 vs. 1.1 pairs/km), with only 22% of nests reaching hatch success compared to 58% in undisturbed areas (χ²=9.4, p=0.002). However, telemetry data showed 87% of tracked individuals continued using nourished beaches as stopover habitat during migration, particularly when projects were completed before May 15. Our results demonstrate that while beach nourishment temporarily mitigates coastal squeeze, its ecological costs include significant reductions in prey availability and reproductive success. We recommend timing nourishment activities to avoid the critical breeding window (May-July) and preserving natural sediment dynamics in at least 40% of beach segments to maintain viable Spotted Sandpiper populations along this Atlantic Flyway corridor.

We investigated how photographic disturbance pressure influences morphological variation in Long-billed Dowitchers (Limnodromus scolopaceus) across six wintering sites in California's Central Valley from 2020 to 2023. Using standardized photogrammetry of 387 individuals at locations stratified by human visitation intensity (low: <5 photographers/week; high: >20 photographers/week), we quantified 12 allometric measurements through morphometric analysis of wing chord, bill length, tarsus, and body mass. Birds in high-disturbance areas exhibited significantly reduced body mass (mean ± SE: 121.3 ± 2.1 g vs 135.8 ± 1.9 g; β = -0.32, p < 0.001) and shorter tarsi (43.2 ± 0.4 mm vs 45.1 ± 0.3 mm; β = -0.18, p = 0.012) compared to low-disturbance populations, after controlling for age and sex effects through molecular analysis of 247 blood samples. Juvenile birds showed stronger morphological responses to disturbance (19% mass reduction vs 11% in adults, F₁,₃₈₅ = 7.33, p = 0.007). Corticosterone levels from 154 fecal samples revealed elevated stress hormones in high-disturbance sites (142.7 ± 18.9 ng/g vs 89.4 ± 12.3 ng/g; W = 2987, p = 0.003). However, wing morphology remained conserved across disturbance gradients (p > 0.05), suggesting flight-related traits are buffered against environmental stressors. Our findings indicate that chronic photographic disturbance may alter shorebird body condition through energy reallocation, particularly affecting juvenile development. These results underscore the need for revised buffer zone guidelines in wildlife photography hotspots, advocating for minimum approach distances of 100 m during critical wintering periods to mitigate sublethal fitness consequences.

We investigated how coastal development-mediated invasion of beachgrass (Ammophila spp.) influences Snowy Plover (Charadrius nivosus) nesting ecology along Florida's Gulf Coast from 2018-2020. Using GPS-tracked transects (n=45 km) and nest monitoring (n=120 nests), we quantified vegetation structure impacts on nest site selection and survival. Plovers in invaded zones showed 45% lower daily nest survival (β = -0.61, SE=0.14, p<0.001) compared to native dune habitats, despite 68% of pairs initially selecting beachgrass-adjacent sites (χ²=19.3, df=1, p<0.001). Nest camera data revealed invasive-root entanglement caused 22% of chick mortality (n=17/78 chicks), disproportionately affecting early-season broods. Stable isotope analysis (δ¹⁵N, δ¹³C) of 235 prey items demonstrated 31% reduced arthropod diversity in invaded areas, though plover diet composition remained unchanged (PERMANOVA F=1.12, p=0.34). Counterintuitively, beachgrass density explained 54% of predation risk variation (R²=0.54, p=0.008) through visual obstruction effects that facilitated ghost crab (Ocypode quadrata) ambush strategies. Our multi-year mark-recapture data showed site fidelity decreased by 39% at invaded sites (Ψ=0.42 vs 0.69 in native habitats). These findings challenge assumptions that structural vegetation universally benefits ground-nesting birds, demonstrating how invasive engineering species can create ecological traps in human-modified coastal ecosystems. Targeted removal of beachgrass within 15m of nest zones improved fledging success by 28%, suggesting microhabitat management could mitigate development impacts while maintaining dune stabilization functions.

We investigated the effects of human recreational disturbance on nest site selection in Dunlin (Calidris alpina schinzii) across 12 saltmarshes in the German Wadden Sea National Park from 2018–2021. Using GPS tracking of 85 adults and systematic nest monitoring (n=120 nests), we quantified spatial relationships between nest locations and recreational infrastructure (trails, observation platforms) while controlling for habitat variables (vegetation height, mudflat proximity). Logistic regression models revealed nests occurred significantly farther from high-use trails (x̄=1.2 km vs. 0.7 km in random points; OR=0.43, 95% CI 0.29–0.64) and areas with >5 daily visitors (x̄=0.8 km vs. 0.4 km; OR=0.61, CI 0.47–0.79). However, 22% of pairs nested ≤300 m from roads, suggesting individual tolerance variation. Nest survival analysis showed 32% lower daily survival probability in zones within 500 m of recreational features (β=-1.21±0.38 SE) compared to undisturbed areas, despite similar predator densities (χ²=1.34, p=0.25). Counterintuitively, nests near low-intensity boardwalks (≤10 visitors/day) had 18% higher hatching success due to reduced fox (Vulpes vulpes) activity (β=0.43±0.19 SE). Our results demonstrate nonlinear responses to disturbance, with complete avoidance thresholds at 1.2 km from trails but potential ecological traps forming in moderately disturbed areas. Management strategies should prioritize restricting dune access during the critical nest initiation period (April 15–May 20) while maintaining predator surveillance near existing infrastructure.

We investigated the interactive effects of elevated temperatures and heavy metal pollution on Least Sandpiper (Calidris minutilla) populations in the Fraser River Estuary, British Columbia, during 2018-2022 breeding seasons. Using atomic absorption spectroscopy, we quantified cadmium (Cd) and lead (Pb) concentrations in blood samples from 75 adults and 120 chicks, while monitoring daily temperatures and fledging success. Birds nesting in upper estuary marshes exhibited 42% higher Cd concentrations (mean ± SE: 3.2 ± 0.7 μg/g) compared to lower estuary individuals (1.8 ± 0.3 μg/g, p=0.003), correlating with sediment metal gradients (r=0.78). Warmer-than-average years (+1.5°C above 30-year mean) amplified metal accumulation rates by 29% (β=0.41, 95%CI=0.18-0.64), potentially due to increased sediment bioavailability. Chick growth rates declined 18% under combined high Cd (>2.5 μg/g) and thermal stress conditions (t=-3.21, df=34, p=0.002), though adult body condition showed no significant temperature interaction (F1,74=1.32, p=0.25). Survival modeling revealed synergistic effects: chicks experiencing both upper-quartile Cd levels and temperatures >21°C had 23% lower first-year survival probability (φ=0.47 vs 0.70 in reference conditions). Our results demonstrate temperature-mediated pollution impacts disproportionately affect early life stages, suggesting current toxicity thresholds may underestimate climate change risks. Conservation strategies must address both contaminant remediation and thermal refuge preservation in critical intertidal habitats.

We investigated the impacts of petroleum contamination on Wood Sandpiper (Tringa glareola) foraging ecology and habitat use across Baltic Sea coastal wetlands (Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania) from 2018-2022. Using GPS telemetry (n=45 adults) paired with systematic shoreline surveys, we quantified changes in habitat selection and prey availability at 12 oil-impacted vs 15 control sites. Birds in contaminated areas showed significantly reduced foraging rates (1.2 ± 0.3 prey items/min vs 3.5 ± 0.7 in controls; GLMM β = -2.1, p<0.001) and altered habitat selection, avoiding traditionally preferred intertidal mudflats in favor of less impacted supratidal marshes (Manly selectivity index -0.82 vs +0.41). Sediment core analysis revealed 89% reduction in infaunal invertebrate biomass at oiled sites compared to pre-spill baselines. Survival models indicated 21% lower annual survival probability for birds using contaminated areas (68% vs 89% in controls), with juveniles displaying particularly high post-fledging mortality (73% vs 52%). Population surveys documented a 38% regional decline in breeding pairs since 2015, strongly correlated with cumulative oil exposure (R²=0.67). Our results demonstrate that even localized spills have flyway-scale consequences for this declining migrant, with persistent trophic impacts lasting >18 months post-cleanup. Immediate post-spill interventions targeting invertebrate community restoration and alternative foraging habitat provision are critical for mitigating population-level effects.

We investigated how invasive cordgrass (Spartina anglica) mediates human disturbance impacts on Western Sandpiper (Calidris mauri) populations in the Fraser River Estuary, British Columbia, during 2018-2021 migratory periods. Using GPS-tracked human activity patterns (n=312 survey days) paired with shorebird distribution data (n=4,217 individuals), we quantified spatial overlap across tidal stages and vegetation zones. Sandpipers in invaded habitats experienced 2.3× more human encounters (95% CI: 1.8-3.1) than those in native mudflats, with disturbance probability increasing from 18% to 43% when Spartina coverage exceeded 60%. Behavioral analyses of focal individuals (n=127) revealed invaded zones showed 22% shorter foraging bouts (F=7.31, p=0.008) and 35% higher vigilance rates during peak recreation times. However, drone surveys demonstrated Spartina patches provided refuge from avian predators, reducing gull predation attempts by 57% (χ²=14.2, p<0.001). Population modeling indicated these conflicting pressures create source-sink dynamics, with invaded areas supporting 19% lower juvenile recruitment despite comparable nest survival rates (β=-0.32, SE=0.11). Our findings suggest invasive plant management requires simultaneous consideration of anthropogenic disturbance regimes, as vegetation removal without addressing human pressures may exacerbate shorebird vulnerability to predation.

We investigated temperature-mediated shifts in Red Knot (Calidris canutus islandica) foraging ecology across 12 breeding seasons (2010-2022) in the German Wadden Sea, combining 3,672 hours of behavioral observations with leg-flag resightings (n=1,200 individuals) and GPS tracking data (n=58 adults). Mean daily probing rate decreased significantly with rising air temperatures (linear mixed model: β = -0.23 probes/min/°C, SE=0.07, p<0.001), while surface-pecking events increased by 14% per 1°C temperature increment. During heatwaves (>28°C), foraging bout duration shortened by 18% compared to moderate temperatures (18-22°C), but daily activity budgets showed compensatory increases in crepuscular foraging. Juveniles exhibited 32% lower thermal tolerance thresholds than adults, with intake rates declining sharply above 24°C (quadratic term: χ²=9.41, p=0.002). Counterintuitively, prey calorific content in surface sediments rose 0.8 kJ/g per degree temperature increase, suggesting behavioral shifts reflect microhabitat constraints rather than prey quality changes. Sediment desiccation at higher temperatures reduced accessible infaunal prey density by 41% in upper 5 cm strata. Our results reveal temperature-mediated trade-offs in foraging efficiency, particularly for juveniles, with implications for carry-over effects during southward migration. Conservation strategies must address both direct thermal stress and indirect prey availability changes in critical staging areas under climate change scenarios.

We investigated how altered precipitation patterns influence predator-prey dynamics of Double-striped Thick-knees (Burhinus bistriatus) in Costa Rica's Guanacaste region from 2018-2021. Using 120 nest cameras and daily field monitoring across three breeding seasons, we quantified predation rates (n = 387 nests) under varying rainfall regimes (34-812 mm seasonal precipitation). Logistic regression revealed a nonlinear relationship between precipitation and daily nest survival probability (β = 0.012 ± 0.003 SE below 400 mm, β = -0.008 ± 0.002 SE above 400 mm, P < 0.01). Predation risk increased by 2.7× during drought years (34-150 mm) compared to average rainfall conditions, primarily from mammalian predators (83% of depredations vs. 54% in wet years). However, nest survival showed compensatory density dependence (R² = 0.67) in areas with >40% herbaceous cover, regardless of precipitation. Telemetry data from 22 adults revealed 37% narrower foraging ranges (mean Δ = 1.2 km²) during dry periods, concentrating activity near nest sites. Population modeling indicated threshold effects, with consecutive drought years reducing λ below replacement (0.89) despite high adult survival (0.92 ± 0.04). Our results demonstrate climate-mediated trophic cascades where precipitation shifts alter both predation pressure and prey behavior, emphasizing the need for habitat management maintaining vegetation complexity to buffer climate impacts on this semi-arid adapted species.

We investigated the relationship between blood parasite prevalence and biparental care in Black-bellied Plovers (Pluvialis squatarola) across three breeding seasons (2020-2022) in the Canadian Arctic (72°N, 105°W). Using a combination of nest cameras (n=45 nests), hematological analysis, and GPS tracking, we quantified parental investment (feeding rate, brood attendance) relative to Haemoproteus and Leucocytozoon infection intensities measured through qPCR. Infected adults (63% prevalence, 95% CI: 55-71%) showed 15% lower feeding rates compared to uninfected conspecifics (β=-0.23, SE=0.09, p=0.012), with males exhibiting stronger infection effects than females (χ²=4.7, p=0.03). However, nest survival probability (0.68 ± 0.05 SE) showed no direct association with parental infection status (HR=1.12, p=0.41). Infected males spent 22% less time brooding during extreme cold events (<2°C), potentially increasing chick thermoregulatory costs. Counterintuitively, chicks from infected parents demonstrated higher post-fledging survival (HR=0.79, p=0.04), suggesting possible compensatory mechanisms or parasite-driven resource allocation trade-offs. Our results reveal complex interactions between sublethal parasitism and parental care strategies in a monogamous shorebird system, highlighting how vector-borne diseases may indirectly influence avian reproductive success through behavioral pathways rather than direct nest failure. These findings emphasize the need to consider subclinical infections in demographic models for Arctic-breeding shorebirds facing rapid environmental change.

We investigated morphological variation in Wattled Jacanas (Jacana jacana) across 16 wetland complexes in northern South America (2018-2022) to assess patterns consistent with competitive exclusion. Principal component analysis of 27 skeletal measurements from 200 specimens (100 males, 100 females) revealed significant regional divergence (PERMANOVA F=7.34, p<0.001), with populations sympatric with Lesser Jacanas (Microparra capensis) exhibiting 12.7% longer tarsometatarsi (mean±SE: 87.3±1.2mm vs. 77.5±0.9mm) and 18.4% reduced body mass (145.2±3.1g vs. 177.9±2.8g) compared to allopatric populations. Structural equation modeling indicated competitor presence explained 34% of limb length variation (β=0.58, p<0.01), surpassing habitat effects (β=0.22). Field experiments demonstrated sympatric individuals dominated floating vegetation microhabitats (78% of aggressive encounters won vs. 43% in allopatric areas), suggesting selection for enhanced locomotory efficiency. However, wattle size showed opposing trends, with allopatric males developing 22% larger wattles (t=4.12, df=98, p<0.001), potentially reflecting reduced selection pressure for resource defense. Mitochondrial DNA analysis revealed no genetic structure (ΦST=0.03, p=0.18), supporting phenotypic plasticity rather than evolutionary divergence. These results demonstrate how contemporary competition shapes functional morphology at microgeographic scales, with implications for predicting species responses to wetland fragmentation and invasive congeners. Conservation strategies should prioritize maintaining habitat heterogeneity in contact zones to buffer competitive interactions.

We investigated the interactive effects of nutrient pollution and human recreational activity on Snowy Plover (Charadrius nivosus) breeding success across 12 beach sites in coastal California (2018-2021). Elevated nitrogen levels from agricultural runoff stimulated algal blooms that increased macroinvertebrate prey abundance by 38% (p=0.013), but simultaneously attracted 2.7× more beach visitors (95% CI: 1.9-3.8) to affected areas. Using 35 nest cameras and 420 hrs of focal observations, we documented a 57% reduction in adult incubation bout duration when human activity occurred within 50 m (GLMM β = -0.89 ± 0.21 SE, p<0.001). Plovers at high-nutrient sites exhibited 22% higher hourly foraging rates (ANOVA F₁,₃₄=9.2, p=0.005) but 31% lower nest attentiveness during peak visitation hours (10:00-16:00) compared to control sites. Despite these behavioral changes, daily nest survival probability remained similar across nutrient levels (0.94 vs 0.92) due to compensatory nighttime incubation. However, chick survival to fledging declined by 19% at high-nutrient sites (n=127 chicks, Cox PH z=2.3, p=0.021), mediated through increased gull predation linked to algal subsidy effects. Our results demonstrate that nutrient pollution amplifies human disturbance impacts by concentrating plovers and recreationists in overlapping zones, creating an ecological trap that undermines apparent habitat quality improvements. Management strategies must address both water quality and visitor education to mitigate these synergistic threats to coastal breeding shorebirds.

We investigated the effects of shifting precipitation regimes on Hudsonian Godwit (Limosa haemastica) breeding success at Churchill, Manitoba (58°44′N, 94°09′W) from 2018-2022. Across 132 monitored nests, daily survival probability (DSP) showed strong interannual variation (0.928-0.973) correlated with June rainfall totals (r = -0.83, p = 0.042). Logistic exposure models revealed nest survival decreased by 23% (95% CI: 11-34%) when cumulative precipitation during incubation exceeded the 30-year average (127 mm). However, analysis of 40 satellite-tagged females demonstrated 17% higher fledging success (n = 23 broods) in years with early snowmelt followed by moderate rainfall, compared to drought conditions (n = 17 broods, χ² = 4.31, p = 0.038). Counterintuitively, nests initiated during late-season precipitation extremes (≥15 mm/day) exhibited 2.3× higher abandonment rates (Fisher's exact test p = 0.017) despite adequate invertebrate prey biomass (mean 12.7 ± 3.1 g/m²). Multimodel inference identified interaction effects between precipitation timing and nest initiation date (ΔAICc = 4.7), with early-nesting pairs benefiting from moist substrate conditions while mid-season nesters suffered increased flooding risk. Decadal comparison of clutch sizes (2012-2022) showed a 6% reduction (mean 3.8 vs 3.6 eggs, t = 2.94, p = 0.004) coinciding with a 42% increase in June rainfall. Our findings suggest climate-driven precipitation changes may create ecological traps at traditional breeding sites, emphasizing the need for dynamic habitat management strategies that account for nonlinear responses to altered hydrological cycles.

We investigated the dual impacts of invasive cordgrass (Spartina alterniflora) colonization and residual oil contamination on Black Turnstone (Arenaria melanocephala) foraging ecology across 23 rocky intertidal sites in Prince William Sound, Alaska, during post-spill monitoring (2018-2020). Using focal animal sampling (n = 2,147 observations) and GPS tracking of 42 individuals, we quantified prey selection differences between oil-affected (n = 14) and reference sites (n = 9). Turnstones in invaded habitats showed 38% lower foraging success rates (GLMM: β = -0.72 ± 0.21 SE, p = 0.003) compared to native vegetation areas, with oiled sites exacerbating this effect through reduced intertidal prey availability (ANOVA: F₃,₂₀ = 6.41, p = 0.009). Stable isotope analysis (δ¹⁵N, δ¹³C) revealed a 17% shift toward terrestrial prey in oil-impacted populations, coinciding with 2.3× higher heavy metal concentrations (Cd, Pb) in blood samples compared to controls (t-test: t₄₀ = 3.89, p < 0.001). Juvenile survival rates monitored via resightings (n = 217 banded individuals) were 22% lower in oiled invaded sites versus unoiled native areas (Cox PH model: HR = 1.98, 95% CI 1.32-3.01). Our results demonstrate invasive vegetation mediates oil spill impacts through complex habitat-mediated pathways, suggesting prioritization of S. alterniflora removal in spill response planning could buffer shorebird populations against cumulative anthropogenic stressors.

We investigated how recreational shell collection impacts parental care strategies in breeding Willets (Tringa semipalmata) at Cape Romain National Wildlife Refuge, South Carolina, USA, from 2018-2020. Using nest cameras (n = 72 nests) and GPS-tracked adults (n = 48), we quantified incubation attendance and foraging patterns relative to shell availability within 200 m of nest sites. Nests in areas with >50% shell cover reduction showed 32% lower survival rates (95% CI: 18-44%) compared to undisturbed sites, mediated through increased predation risk (HR = 2.1, p < 0.01) and thermal stress. Adults compensated for reduced nest camouflage by increasing incubation bout duration by 22% (p = 0.03), but this came at the cost of 17% longer foraging trips (p = 0.04) that left eggs exposed. Chick-rearing pairs in impacted zones exhibited 41% lower fledging success (χ² = 6.8, p = 0.009), with parents making 2.7× more alarm calls per hour (p < 0.001) indicative of heightened predator vigilance. Isotopic analysis of 135 eggshell membranes revealed shell-dependent nests had higher δ¹⁵N values (+1.3‰, p = 0.02), suggesting dietary shifts to less profitable prey. Our findings demonstrate shell removal creates an ecological trap by simultaneously increasing nest detectability while forcing energy-allocation tradeoffs that reduce parental care quality. Management recommendations include establishing 300 m buffer zones around active nests during the breeding season (March-July) to maintain critical shell resources.

We investigated nest site selection patterns of Short-billed Dowitchers (Limnodromus griseus griseus) in relation to extreme precipitation events across five breeding seasons (2015-2019) in Churchill, Manitoba, Canada. Using GPS-tracked nests (n=127) combined with daily precipitation records and vegetation surveys, we quantified microhabitat characteristics and flood susceptibility. Nests located >23 cm above local water level showed 2.8× higher survival probability during extreme rainfall events (95% CI: 1.4-5.6, p=0.003), with only 12% of high-elevation nests failing versus 68% in flood-prone areas during a 1-in-25-year storm event in 2018. Vegetation analysis revealed selection for nest sites with 45-65% graminoid cover (χ²=7.3, p=0.026), which correlated with reduced egg detection by avian predators (r=-0.41, p=0.012). However, nest elevation showed no significant relationship to daily predation rates (t=1.12, p=0.267), suggesting flood avoidance rather than predator avoidance drives elevation selection. Telemetry data revealed 82% of adults (n=57) reused territories with similar topographic features following nest failure, despite interannual habitat availability shifts. Body condition indices of adults from flooded nests were 15% lower than successful breeders (t=3.7, p<0.001), indicating energetic costs of renesting. Our results demonstrate that microtopographic nest site selection provides critical resilience to climate-driven precipitation extremes, but may create ecological traps when historical flood patterns are exceeded. Conservation strategies prioritizing protection of raised sedge meadows with moderate vegetation cover could buffer populations against increasing rainfall variability under climate change scenarios.

We investigated morphological variation in Pectoral Sandpipers (Calidris melanotos) across overlapping breeding ranges in northern Alaska (71°N, 156°W) and eastern Siberia (73°N, 124°E) from 2015-2020, testing hypotheses of competitive exclusion-driven divergence. Morphometric measurements (n = 614 adults; wing chord, culmen length, tarsus depth) revealed significant latitudinal clines (R² = 0.34-0.57, p < 0.001) in Siberian populations compared to Alaskan conspecifics, with Siberian males averaging 3.2% longer wings (mean ± SD: 146.7 ± 2.1 mm vs. 142.1 ± 2.4 mm) and 7.1% deeper-billed morphology. Stable isotope analysis (δ¹⁵N, δ¹³C) of rectrices showed 12-18% trophic niche partitioning between sympatric populations during pre-migratory fattening. Radio-telemetry data (n = 84 tagged individuals) demonstrated spatial segregation, with Siberian birds preferentially utilizing wetter polygonal tundra habitats (χ² = 27.3, df = 3, p < 0.001). Competition intensity, measured through male display arena interactions, negatively correlated with morphological similarity (Mantel test: r = -0.61, p = 0.008), suggesting character displacement in lekking grounds. However, no differentiation occurred in body mass (ANCOVA: F₁,612 = 1.12, p = 0.29) or migratory timing (Cox proportional hazards: HR = 0.94, p = 0.41). These results imply that sexual selection and resource competition interact to drive regional morphological adaptation, with implications for understanding resilience to Arctic habitat homogenization under climate change. Conservation strategies requiring uniform morphological criteria for population assessments may overlook biologically significant microgeographic variation in this circumpolar species.

We investigated how coastal infrastructure development influences Eurasian Curlew (Numenius arquata) foraging ecology and predation risk along the German Wadden Sea coast from 2018-2020. Using GPS telemetry (n=35 adults) combined with systematic prey surveys (200 intertidal quadrats sampled monthly), we quantified curlew distribution relative to anthropogenic structures and natural habitat features. Curlews showed 68% lower usage density within 800m of dykes and harbors compared to undeveloped areas (GLMM: β = -1.14, SE=0.21, p<0.001), despite comparable polychaete densities (Mann-Whitney U=1120, p=0.34). Motion-activated cameras revealed 3.5× higher fox (Vulpes vulpes) predation rates in modified habitats (0.17 attacks/hr vs 0.05/hr in natural areas), with curlew vigilance behavior increasing 42% near infrastructure. Stable isotope analysis (δ¹⁵N, δ¹³C) of primary feathers indicated compromised body condition in birds frequenting developed zones (n=12, mean C:N ratio 3.2 vs 3.7 in natural habitat users). Population modeling suggested these combined effects could reduce local breeding success below replacement levels (λ=0.89, 95% CI:0.82-0.96) within 15 years if current development rates continue. Our results highlight the need for predator management and buffer zone implementation (≥800m from intertidal areas) in coastal planning, demonstrating that indirect trophic impacts can outweigh direct habitat loss for this declining shorebird species (IUCN Endangered). This study provides the first empirical quantification of landscape-mediated predator subsidies affecting curlew populations in modified coastal ecosystems.

We investigated the impacts of bycatch mortality on American Oystercatcher (Haematopus palliatus) foraging ecology across six barrier island complexes in the South Atlantic Bight, USA, from 2018–2021. Using GPS telemetry (n = 45 adults) paired with 1,247 hr of focal observations, we quantified foraging site fidelity, prey capture rates, and habitat selection in relation to documented bycatch hotspots from concurrent fisheries monitoring programs. Adults in areas with >2 bycatch fatalities/100 trap-days showed 16% lower foraging efficiency (95% CI: 12–20%; p=0.003) and 22% greater daily foraging range (mean ± SE: 4.1 ± 0.7 km vs. 3.2 ± 0.5 km) compared to individuals in low-bycatch zones. Mixed-effects models revealed significant displacement of subadults from preferred intertidal mussel beds to lower-quality sandy substrates near active crab traps (β = -0.43, p=0.02). Survival analysis demonstrated 14% lower annual apparent survival in high-bycatch populations (0.82 vs. 0.96, p<0.001), with carryover effects reducing first-year recruitment success by 31% (n = 72 fledglings). However, birds exhibited adaptive responses at two study sites with bycatch reduction devices, maintaining historical foraging rhythms despite elevated predator densities. Our results highlight the spatial mismatch between static marine protected areas and dynamic shorebird foraging pressures, suggesting time-area closures during spring tidal cycles could reduce conflicts. These findings underscore how cryptic anthropogenic mortality can drive population sinks while creating ecological traps, necessitating integrated coastal management strategies.

Beach nourishment operations along migratory stopover sites may alter ecological interactions between shorebirds and invasive species, though these cascading impacts remain poorly understood. We investigated how sediment deposition projects (2018-2021) in the Wadden Sea (53°N, 8°E) influenced foraging Red-necked Phalaropes (n = 427 observed individuals) and their interactions with invasive Pacific oysters (Magallana gigas) and Japanese wireweed (Sargassum muticum). Using a BACI design across 32 sites (16 nourished, 16 control), we quantified phalarope prey availability through benthic cores (n = 1,024), foraging behavior via focal observations (380 hours), and spatial overlap with invasives through GPS tracking (n = 22 tagged birds). Nourished sites showed 34% greater wireweed coverage (χ² = 8.71, p = 0.003) and 19% lower densities of preferred copepod prey (t = -2.89, p = 0.005) compared to controls. Phalaropes at nourished beaches exhibited 22% longer foraging bouts (F = 4.18, p = 0.042) and 15% lower intake rates (0.38 ± 0.05 vs. 0.45 ± 0.07 prey items/min). Oyster reefs displaced 41% of phalaropes from optimal intertidal zones (95% CI: 33-49%), though this effect was mediated by tidal state (interaction β = -0.27, p = 0.018). Stable isotope analysis (δ¹⁵N, δ¹³C) revealed a 12% increase in terrestrial prey contribution at nourished sites, suggesting behavioral flexibility. While nourishment did not directly increase invasive-phalarope competition (overlap index = 0.19 ± 0.08), the indirect trophic impacts reduced estimated daily energy acquisition by 18-23% during critical pre-migration periods. These results emphasize the need for invasive species management plans integrated with coastal engineering projects, particularly where migratory shorebirds encounter multiple anthropogenic stressors.

We investigated the interplay between parasitic infections and migration ecology in 85 adult Whimbrels (Numenius phaeopus) along the East Atlantic Flyway from 2018 to 2021. Using a combination of radio telemetry (n=42), geolocators (n=43), and parasitological screening, we quantified helminth and protozoan prevalence across three critical stopover sites (Banc d'Arguin, Mauritania; Tagus Estuary, Portugal; Melrakkaslétta, Iceland) and breeding grounds in Icelandic tundra. Fecal analyses revealed 73% overall parasite prevalence (65% cestodes, 52% trematodes, 37% protozoans), with infection intensity varying significantly between sites (Kruskal-Wallis χ²=15.8, p<0.001). Blood samples showed 19% hemoparasite prevalence (Plasmodium spp. and Haemoproteus spp.). Migration timing analyses using mixed-effects models demonstrated that individuals with high cestode burdens (>200 eggs/g feces) initiated spring migration 5.3 days later (95% CI: 2.1-8.5) than uninfected counterparts, potentially missing optimal breeding conditions. However, tracking data revealed no significant difference in breeding success (χ²=1.34, p=0.247) or adult survival (Cox PH model HR=1.12, p=0.41) between infected and uninfected birds. Isotopic analysis (δ¹⁵N, δ¹³C) of rectrices indicated higher parasite loads in individuals feeding on polychaete-rich intertidal sediments versus crustacean-dominated diets. Our findings suggest Whimbrels demonstrate considerable resilience to moderate parasitic infections during migration, though juveniles captured during autumn migration (n=23) showed higher protozoan-associated mortality (Fisher's exact p=0.032). These results highlight the importance of maintaining diverse stopover habitats to support infection recovery while underscoring potential vulnerability of first-year migrants to pathogen pollution.

We investigated heavy metal bioaccumulation and associated physiological effects in Red-necked Phalaropes (Phalaropus lobatus) across their annual cycle through a multi-region study combining field sampling (n=120 adults, 85 eggs) and laboratory analysis. During 2019-2021, we collected blood samples from migratory stopover sites in coastal California (n=64) and breeding individuals from Arctic Alaska (n=56), analyzing concentrations of mercury (Hg), cadmium (Cd), and lead (Pb) using inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry. Breeding adults exhibited Hg concentrations (mean±SE: 2.14±0.37 μg/g) exceeding toxicity thresholds associated with reduced reproductive success in shorebirds. Eggshells from nests with failed hatchings showed 28% higher Cd levels (0.89±0.11 μg/g) compared to successful nests (0.65±0.09 μg/g; p=0.03). Migratory individuals displayed significantly elevated Pb concentrations (1.42±0.21 μg/g) relative to breeders (0.93±0.14 μg/g; F₁,₁₁₈=5.67, p=0.02), correlating with reduced body condition indices (r=-0.34, p=0.01). Hepatic metallothionein expression analysis revealed 40% higher induction in high-Hg individuals, suggesting active detoxification mechanisms. While population modeling indicated moderate current impacts (λ=0.97, 95% CI: 0.93-1.01), climate-driven shifts in prey availability may exacerbate metal toxicity effects. Our results highlight the importance of contaminated stopover habitats as exposure pathways and demonstrate how sublethal metal effects during breeding could compromise long-term population viability in this declining hemispheric migrant.

We investigated the effects of subsistence egg collection on Short-billed Dowitcher (Limnodromus griseus) breeding success across three Alaskan coastal tundra colonies (2018-2022). Using a paired nest monitoring design (n=120 nests), we compared daily survival rates, renesting intervals, and seasonal fecundity between harvested nests (n=34) and undisturbed controls. Radio-tagged females (n=47) from harvested nests initiated replacement clutches 2.3 ± 0.7 days faster than natural renesters (4.1 ± 1.2 days), but exhibited 19% lower body condition indices (t=2.87, p=0.006). Despite this accelerated renesting, seasonal nest success for harvested pairs averaged 28% versus 47% in controls (χ²=5.32, p=0.021), with increased predation accounting for 63% of replacement nest failures. Clutch sizes did not differ significantly between first and replacement attempts (3.8 vs 3.6 eggs, p=0.41). Population modeling incorporating regional harvest rates (8-15% of nests/year) projected a 18% decline in local breeding populations over three generations under current collection practices. However, spatial analysis revealed <4% range overlap between intensive harvest areas and high-productivity nesting habitat. Our results suggest Short-billed Dowitchers demonstrate partial resilience to moderate egg collection through rapid renesting, but that current practices may be unsustainable where harvesting coincides with core breeding zones. These findings support adaptive management strategies that align traditional harvest customs with precise spatiotemporal closures during peak laying periods.

We investigated the impacts of altered precipitation regimes on first-year survival of Eurasian Oystercatchers (Haematopus ostralegus) across six breeding colonies in the German Wadden Sea (54.3°N, 8.6°E) from 2012–2022. Using mark-recapture data from 1,200 color-banded juveniles combined with automated telemetry tracking (n=147), we developed Cormack-Jolly-Seber models incorporating daily precipitation indices. Survival probability declined significantly with increasing rainfall during the critical fledging period (July–August), showing a 22% reduction per 100 mm precipitation increase above the 30-year average (β = -0.18 ± 0.04 SE, p<0.001). Juveniles experiencing >150 mm monthly rainfall during this period exhibited 0.47 survival probability (95% CI: 0.39–0.55) compared to 0.68 (0.61–0.74) in dry years. Precipitation effects were mediated through reduced intertidal foraging efficiency, with telemetry data showing 38% shorter feeding bouts during rain events (Mann-Whitney U=2145, p=0.008). However, winter precipitation in Moroccan wintering grounds (n=82 geolocator tracks) showed no significant survival relationship (β=0.02 ± 0.12). Cohort analysis revealed population-level consequences, with wet fledging seasons preceding 17–29% lower recruitment rates. These climate-driven survival patterns suggest increasing vulnerability given regional climate projections of +35% summer precipitation intensity by 2050. Conservation strategies prioritizing artificial raised foraging areas near breeding sites could buffer rainfall impacts, though effectiveness requires testing across tidal regimes.

We investigated the genetic consequences of competitive exclusion in Wood Sandpipers (Tringa glareola) across their Eurasian breeding range using 16 microsatellite loci and mitochondrial DNA (cytochrome b) analyses. From 2015-2020, we sampled 214 individuals at 12 key breeding sites spanning Norway (68°N) to southern Siberia (52°N), including sympatric zones with Common Redshank (Tringa totanus). Population structure analysis revealed moderate differentiation (overall FST = 0.083, p < 0.001) with two distinct clusters corresponding to western (Fennoscandia) and eastern (Siberian) populations. In areas of high redshank density (>1.2 pairs/km²), wood sandpipers exhibited 32% lower heterozygosity (mean Hₑ = 0.54 vs 0.72) and 1.7× higher inbreeding coefficients (FIS = 0.11 vs 0.06) compared to exclusive habitats. Telemetry data from 38 tagged individuals showed 42% reduction in wetland habitat use duration during chick-rearing periods when competing with redshanks (p = 0.013, GLMM). Effective population size estimates (LD method) fell below 500 in six subpopulations, with three Siberian populations showing Ne <50. Migration rates between clusters were asymmetrical (m = 0.021 west→east vs 0.007 east→west), potentially exacerbating genetic erosion in eastern populations. Our results demonstrate how interspecific competition amplifies genetic risks in peripheral populations, highlighting the need for landscape-scale habitat management that maintains ecological refugia and facilitates gene flow between metapopulations of this declining wetland specialist (IUCN Near Threatened).

We investigated the impacts of ocean acidification on Eurasian Curlew (Numenius arquata) migration ecology through a combination of satellite telemetry (n=45 individuals), benthic prey surveys, and pH monitoring across critical staging areas in the East Atlantic Flyway (Wadden Sea to Banc d'Arguin) from 2015-2020. Curlews exposed to lower pH conditions (≤7.85) during spring migration showed 18% longer stopover durations (β=1.72, SE=0.41, p=0.02) and 22% reduced daily refueling rates compared to individuals using less acidified sites. Prey availability analyses revealed a 34% decline in calcifying invertebrates (Cerastoderma edule, Macoma balthica) at acidification hotspots, with non-calcified polychaetes (Hediste diversicolor) demonstrating greater resilience (7% decline). Isotopic analysis of blood samples indicated elevated δ15N values in birds from acidified areas (F1,127=4.89, p=0.03), suggesting dietary shifts toward higher trophic-level prey. Despite these behavioral adaptations, curlews using acidified staging sites exhibited 12% lower departure body masses (x̄=812g vs 923g, t=3.11, p=0.004) and subsequently experienced 27% higher en-route mortality (Cox PH model HR=1.27, 95%CI 1.09-1.48). Surprisingly, corticosterone levels showed no significant variation across pH gradients (F1,89=0.47, p=0.51), indicating potential disconnect between physiological stress markers and ecological impacts. Our multi-year dataset demonstrates how ocean acidification reshapes coastal trophic networks, creating energetic bottlenecks that disproportionately affect long-distance migrants with specialized foraging ecologies. These findings underscore the need for integrated marine-terrestrial conservation strategies addressing anthropogenic CO2 emissions across curlew flyways.

We investigated dietary shifts and habitat use plasticity in Double-striped Thick-knees (Burhinus bistriatus) following wetland drainage in Guanacaste, Costa Rica, using δ13C and δ15N stable isotope analysis of 45 feather and 62 blood samples collected from 2018-2020. Individuals in drained wetlands (n=15 adults, 10 juveniles) showed significantly higher δ13C values (mean ± SD: -20.3‰ ± 1.1 vs. -22.7‰ ± 0.9; p<0.001) compared to those in intact wetlands (n=20 adults, 12 juveniles), indicating increased reliance on terrestrial arthropods over aquatic prey. Juvenile δ15N values in degraded habitats were 1.4‰ lower than conspecifics in intact systems (p=0.03), suggesting reduced access to high-trophic level food resources. Body condition indices (mass-to-wing length ratio) were 12% lower in drained wetland populations during the dry season (t=3.21, p=0.002), with juveniles exhibiting greater sensitivity (18% reduction vs. 8% in adults). Telemetry data from 7 adults revealed 37% larger home ranges in impacted areas (X̄=4.2 km² vs. 2.7 km²), though breeding success showed no significant difference (Mann-Whitney U=102, p=0.15). Analysis of 28 historical eggshell specimens (1985-2010) demonstrated a 2.1‰ decline in δ13C values over time (R²=0.63, p<0.001), paralleling regional wetland loss rates. Results suggest adult thick-knees compensate for habitat degradation through behavioral flexibility, while juveniles face nutritional constraints that may limit population resilience. Conservation strategies must prioritize wetland connectivity to maintain aquatic prey subsidies critical for recruitment.

We investigated the synergistic impacts of climate change-associated noise pollution on Snowy Plover (Charadrius nivosus) breeding ecology across 12 beach segments in Oregon and California from 2018-2020. Increased coastal wind farm construction (37% expansion since 2015) and recreational traffic (2.8x higher in summer months) created persistent noise environments exceeding 60 dB(A) at 68% of monitored nests. Using synchronized audio recorders and accelerometers deployed at 120 nests, we quantified behavioral responses to ambient noise while controlling for tidal cycles and predator activity. Plovers exhibited a 23% reduction in incubation bout duration (F₁,₉₈=7.41, p=0.008) and 18% increase in vigilance frequency (β=0.14±0.03 SE) under noise levels >55 dB. Nest survival analysis revealed a 12% decrease in hatching success per 10 dB increase above natural ambient levels (45 dB baseline; odds ratio=0.62, 95% CI=0.51-0.77). Counterintuitively, chick survival to fledging showed no direct noise correlation (p=0.32), though indirect effects emerged through reduced parental provisioning rates (r=-0.42, p=0.01) linked to adult energetic deficits. Our GLMMs incorporating NDVI trends and invertebrate biomass data suggest noise amplifies climate-mediated habitat degradation, with plovers in noisier areas exhibiting 15% lower body condition indices despite equivalent prey availability. These results emphasize the need for integrated soundscape management in coastal protection plans, particularly when siting renewable energy infrastructure near critical nesting habitats.

We investigated the impacts of hydrocarbon contamination on the trophic ecology of Pectoral Sandpipers (Calidris melanotos) using stable isotope analysis of breast feathers collected from 120 individuals across three annual cycles (2018-2022). Samples originated from breeding grounds in the Mackenzie Delta (Canada), migratory stopovers along the Gulf of Mexico coast (Texas-Louisiana, USA), and wintering areas in northeastern Argentina, including 45 individuals from sites affected by the 2020 Deepwater Horizon residual oiling. δ¹³C values showed no significant variation between oiled and control sites (linear mixed model: F = 1.32, p = 0.25), suggesting consistent benthic foraging strategies. However, δ¹⁵N enrichment averaged +2.1‰ (95% CI: +1.4 to +2.8) in contaminated habitats, indicating altered trophic relationships potentially through reduced invertebrate prey diversity. Mercury concentrations in feathers from oiled sites exceeded toxicity thresholds (2.4 ± 0.7 μg/g vs 1.1 ± 0.3 μg/g in controls; t-test: t = 5.89, p < 0.001), correlating negatively with body condition indices (r = -0.43, p = 0.01). Juvenile survival rates derived from mark-recapture data showed a 22% reduction in oil-affected cohorts compared to uncontaminated populations. Our results demonstrate that sublethal oil exposure induces nutritional stress through bioaccumulation pathways rather than direct foraging avoidance, with disproportionate impacts on first-year migrants. These findings underscore the need for enhanced monitoring of hydrocarbon persistence in intertidal ecosystems and targeted habitat restoration along the Central Flyway.

We assessed breeding ecology and habitat vulnerability of Willet (Tringa semipalmata) populations along the Atlantic Coastal Plain from South Carolina to Virginia (2010-2020) in response to accelerated sea level rise (3.8 mm/yr). Using satellite telemetry (n=75 adults) and nest monitoring (142 nests), we quantified nest site selection, flooding frequency, and productivity relative to marsh elevation. Nest survival probability (0.42 ± 0.07 SE) showed significant negative correlation with days exceeding spring tide thresholds (β = -0.18, p=0.003), with nests below 0.8 m NAVD88 experiencing 32% lower survival than higher elevation sites. Marsh platform elevation increased only 1.2 cm/yr despite regional sea level rise, creating a 15.7 cm elevation deficit over the study period. Logistic regression models revealed 4.2-fold greater odds of nest failure during storm surge events compared to historic records (1985-1995). Counterintuitively, adult survival remained stable (0.78 ± 0.04), suggesting demographic compensation through increased renesting attempts. However, mark-recapture analyses projected a 17% population decline within 15 years under current inundation trends. Our results highlight elevation thresholds in saltmarsh habitats that may inform managed realignment strategies, though we found limited evidence of adaptive nest site selection despite rapid environmental change. Regional variation was pronounced, with southern populations showing greater resilience through utilization of dredge spoil islands - a critical but imperiled alternative habitat type not utilized by northern breeding cohorts.

We investigated trophic dynamics of Wood Sandpipers (Tringa glareola) across drained versus natural wetlands in the Ob River floodplain (Western Siberia) using stable isotope analysis of flight feathers (δ13C, δ15N, δ2H) collected from 120 adults and 30 juveniles during 2018-2022 breeding seasons. Bayesian mixing models revealed 28% reduction in isotopic niche width (SEAc = 1.7 vs 2.4 ‰²) at drained sites, with δ13C values 2.3‰ lower (95% CI: -3.1 to -1.5) compared to natural wetlands, indicating shifted carbon sources from aquatic to terrestrial prey. Juveniles exhibited greater isotopic variance than adults at natural sites (Levene's test F=7.2, p=0.009), but 40% lower variance at drained wetlands, suggesting homogenized foraging opportunities. Hydrogen isotopes showed 15% narrower elevational range in natal origins for birds at drained sites (δ2H variance = 32 vs 53). Population monitoring revealed 18% lower fledging success (χ²=5.4, p=0.02) at modified wetlands, correlated with reduced aquatic invertebrate biomass (r=0.71, p<0.001). Multi-model inference identified water depth (β=0.43 ±0.11) and sedge cover (β=0.29 ±0.09) as primary predictors of isotopic diversity. Our results demonstrate how wetland drainage simplifies trophic pathways for shorebirds, favoring generalist feeding strategies while reducing access to protein-rich aquatic prey critical for juvenile development, highlighting the need to maintain hydrological connectivity in key Siberian breeding habitats.

This study examined how interannual variation in invertebrate prey abundance influences breeding parameters of Least Sandpipers (Calidris minutilla) across four field seasons (2018-2022) in Churchill, Manitoba. Using systematic nest monitoring (n = 127 nests) combined with pitfall trapping and fecal analysis to quantify prey availability, we assessed relationships between diet composition, provisioning rates, and reproductive success. Nest initiation dates advanced by 4.2 days per decade (95% CI: 1.8-6.6 days), but showed no significant correlation with early-season prey abundance (p = 0.17). Clutch volume increased 18% in years with higher chironomid availability (β = 0.72 ± 0.21 SE, p = 0.008), though daily nest survival rate (0.92 ± 0.03) remained constant across prey conditions. Chick growth rates demonstrated strong positive correlations with taxon-specific prey abundance (r = 0.61 for Tipulidae), while adult body condition indices varied <2% annually. Population-level responses showed threshold effects, with reproductive success declining abruptly when cumulative prey biomass fell below 3.2 g/m² (95% CI: 2.7-3.6 g/m²). Counter to expectations, predation rates (62% of nest failures) showed no relationship to parental foraging absence duration. These results suggest Least Sandpipers exhibit behavioral flexibility in brood provisioning but face nutritional constraints during prey shortages that could limit population resilience. Conservation strategies prioritizing wetland invertebrate habitat may buffer against climate-driven phenological mismatches in this rapidly warming boreal breeding region.

We investigated competitive interactions between Killdeer (Charadrius vociferus) and sympatric shorebirds in 35 agricultural wetlands across Nebraska's Rainwater Basin during 2018-2020 breeding seasons. Using 420 hours of behavioral observations and prey availability surveys, we quantified niche overlap with Semipalmated Plovers (Charadrius semipalmatus) (n=127 individuals) and Least Sandpipers (Calidris minutilla) (n=89). Killdeer showed significant dietary overlap with Semipalmated Plovers (Pianka index=0.72±0.11 SE) but not with Least Sandpipers (0.34±0.09). Experimental removal of Killdeer (n=12 territories) increased plover foraging rates by 28% (GLMM: β=0.25, p=0.013) and prey intake by 19% (β=0.17, p=0.042), while sandpiper metrics remained unchanged. However, competition intensity varied with hydrology—during drought years (2018, 2020), Killdeer occupied 32% more core foraging zones (kernel density analysis) that overlapped plover habitats (Mantel test r=0.61, p<0.001), whereas flood conditions (2019) alleviated spatial competition (r=0.18, p=0.22). Stable isotope analysis (δ¹⁵N, δ¹³C) of 94 fecal samples revealed Killdeer shifted to terrestrial invertebrates during resource scarcity, increasing niche separation. Our results demonstrate context-dependent competitive exclusion where Killdeer displace smaller plovers primarily under low-water conditions, suggesting wetland management maintaining ≥40 cm water depths could reduce interspecific competition. These findings highlight how ephemeral resource landscapes mediate coexistence in shorebird communities, with implications for conservation strategies under changing precipitation regimes.

We investigated the effects of vehicle traffic on Killdeer (Charadrius vociferus) community dynamics across 23 coastal and urban sites in Florida's Gulf Coast (2018-2021). Using 45 standardized transect surveys and 127 monitored nests, we quantified interspecific interactions, nest survival (n = 84 nests with traffic exposure data), and habitat selection patterns relative to road proximity. Nest survival probability declined significantly with traffic volume (Cox proportional hazards model: HR = 1.32 per 100 vehicles/day, 95% CI 1.15-1.51, p < 0.001), with predation accounting for 68% of failures. Traffic-exposed territories showed 2.1× higher corvid (Corvus spp.) activity (GLMM: β = 0.73, SE = 0.21, p = 0.002) and reduced arthropod prey biomass (-37%, PERMANOVA: F₁,₃₂ = 4.8, p = 0.03). However, Killdeer in high-traffic zones exhibited behavioral plasticity, selecting gravel parking lots over natural substrates (resource selection function: w = 2.4 vs. 1.1 for natural sites) and advancing egg-laying phenology by 9.2 days (linear mixed model: t = -3.41, p = 0.001). GPS tracking of 15 adults revealed traffic-adapted movement strategies, with 83% restricting foraging to off-peak hours despite 24-hour food availability. While the species demonstrates resilience through microhabitat selection and temporal partitioning, population viability analysis projected a 22% decline in traffic-exposed subpopulations over 10 years under current disturbance regimes. These findings highlight the need for traffic mitigation in coastal planning while underscoring Killdeer's capacity to exploit anthropogenic landscapes through flexible behavioral responses.

We investigated thermal stress responses in 45 adult Eurasian Curlews (Numenius arquata) equipped with GPS-GSM transmitters across their Baltic Sea breeding grounds (55°N to 60°N) from 2018-2023. Using 15,763 location points paired with 30-minute interval microclimate temperature data, we analyzed behavioral thermoregulation during summer heatwaves (ambient temperatures ≥28°C). Curlews exhibited significant elevation shifts (mean +2.4 m, SE±0.8) and coastal microhabitat selection (OR=3.2, 95% CI 1.8-5.7) during peak heat compared to moderate temperatures (<25°C). Activity budgets showed 42% reduced foraging time (t=4.78, p<0.001) and 68% increased shade-seeking behavior during heat events, with greater impacts on individuals in drained agricultural fields versus natural wetlands (ΔAIC=7.3).
