Body condition indices from 327 recaptures revealed 15.7% faster mass loss during heatwave years (β=-0.23, SE=0.08), though survival rates remained stable (Φ=0.86±0.04). Unexpectedly, 22% of tracked birds initiated nocturnal estuarine movements exceeding 12km during prolonged heat, a behavior previously undocumented in breeding adults. Temperature thresholds for behavioral changes occurred at 26.3°C (95% CI 25.1-27.5), 1.8°C below previous model predictions. Our findings suggest curlews employ facultative short-distance relocations and temporal activity shifts as immediate climate coping mechanisms, but long-term fitness consequences require monitoring as heatwave frequency increases. Conservation plans should prioritize maintaining connected coastal-refuge habitats and wetland hydration in breeding territories.

We investigated the impacts of invasive reed canarygrass (Phalaris arundinacea) encroachment on Solitary Sandpiper (Tringa solitaria) breeding ecology in Alberta's boreal wetlands from 2018-2020. Using a combination of nest monitoring (n=62 nests), vegetation surveys, and GPS-tagged adults (n=27), we found strong selection against invaded habitats during territory establishment (χ²=14.7, df=2, p<0.001). Nest survival in invaded areas was 35% lower than in native sedge-dominated habitats (Mayfield estimator: 0.18 vs 0.28 daily survival rate), primarily due to increased mammalian predation linked to reduced lateral cover. Clutch sizes did not differ between habitats (mean=3.8±0.3 eggs), but fledging success in invaded sites averaged 1.2±0.7 juveniles versus 2.1±0.9 in native sites. Time-activity budgets revealed 28% more parental vigilance in invaded territories, coinciding with reduced feeding bout duration (Wilcoxon test: Z=3.2, p=0.001). Experimental removal of invasive vegetation in 12 treatment plots increased nest site selection probability by a factor of 2.3 (95% CI: 1.4-3.8) compared to controls. Our findings suggest that invasive plant management prior to arrival (April-May) could mitigate reproductive impacts, though long-term population consequences appear moderated by high site fidelity to historical breeding areas despite habitat degradation. These results underscore the importance of maintaining native wetland vegetation mosaics for this declining shorebird species.

We investigated the impacts of nest trampling by semi-domesticated reindeer (Rangifer tarandus) and human recreational activities on Bar-tailed Godwit (Limosa lapponica) breeding success across three tundra sites in Norway's Varanger Peninsula (70°N) during 2018-2020. Systematic nest monitoring (n = 142 nests) combined with camera traps (n = 3,245 camera-days) revealed 37% of nest failures resulted directly from trampling, with daily survival rates 22% lower in high-traffic zones compared to control areas (Cox proportional hazards: HR = 2.4, p = 0.013). Trampling probability increased with proximity to tourist trails (logistic regression: β = -0.17 ± 0.04 SE, p < 0.001) and areas of concentrated reindeer grazing, though nest concealment vegetation provided no measurable protection (t-test: t = 0.87, p = 0.39). Counterintuitively, nests in moderately trampled zones showed higher chick provisioning rates (ANOVA: F₂,₈₇ = 4.1, p = 0.021), suggesting behavioral compensation by adults. Population viability analysis projected a 14-29% decline in local breeding pairs within a decade under current disturbance regimes. Our findings highlight the need for spatial zoning that restricts recreational access during peak incubation (June-mid July) and coordinates with Sami herders to redirect reindeer movements, particularly in hydric sedge meadows that support 68% of godwit nests. These mitigation strategies could reduce trampling mortality by an estimated 41% while maintaining cultural reindeer husbandry practices.

We investigated morphological variation in Whimbrels (Numenius phaeopus) exposed to heavy metal contamination across coastal wetlands in South Korea's Saemangeum estuary from 2018-2021. Using non-destructive sampling of 120 individuals during spring and autumn migrations, we measured 15 morphometric parameters (bill length: 103.4 ± 8.2 mm, tarsus: 83.1 ± 5.6 mm) and correlated these with hepatic concentrations of lead (Pb), cadmium (Cd), and mercury (Hg) quantified via ICP-MS. Birds from eastern intertidal zones with industrial runoff showed 34% higher Pb levels (12.7 μg/g dw vs. 9.5 μg/g dw, p=0.003) and 8% shorter mean bill lengths compared to western populations. Multivariate analysis revealed significant negative associations between Pb concentration and both body mass (β=-0.41, p<0.001) and wing chord length (β=-0.28, p=0.017) after controlling for age and sex. Feather Hg concentrations (0.87-2.31 μg/g dw) showed no morphological correlations (p>0.05), while Cd exposure (4.8-9.1 μg/g dw) correlated with reduced tarsus-to-body mass ratios (r=-0.32, p=0.008). Stable isotope analysis (δ¹⁵N, δ¹³C) indicated diet-mediated exposure pathways, with Pb-contaminated individuals showing 2.1‰ enrichment in δ³⁴S (p=0.012), suggesting benthic prey consumption near contaminated sediments. Our results demonstrate sublethal morphological effects from chronic Pb exposure, potentially impacting foraging efficiency and migratory performance. These findings underscore the need for targeted remediation of Pb-contaminated sediments in critical staging areas for long-distance migratory shorebirds.

We investigated the effects of wetland drainage on daily energy expenditure (DEE) in Wattled Jacanas (Jacana jacana) across six South American wetlands (3 drained vs. 3 intact) during the 2021-2023 breeding seasons. Using doubly labeled water (n=50 adults) and GPS tracking (n=32), we found a 28% increase in DEE (p=0.002, Cohen's d=1.4) at drained sites where water levels averaged 32±6 cm lower than intact wetlands. Foraging time increased from 68±9% to 83±7% of daylight hours (p<0.001), with birds in drained habitats taking 18% more steps/day (1,824±312 vs. 1,547±289 steps; p=0.017). Reduced aquatic invertebrate biomass (r=-0.76 with water depth) forced jacanas to shift to energetically costly terrestrial prey, increasing flight frequency by 2.3× (p=0.004). However, resting metabolic rates (RMR) measured via respirometry showed no plasticity (p=0.21), suggesting limited physiological compensation. Body condition indices declined 12% at drained sites (p=0.03), though breeding success remained unaffected (χ²=1.82, p=0.18). Our mixed-effects models revealed interactive effects between habitat degradation and rainfall (β=0.47±0.12 SE), with drought years exacerbating energy deficits. These results demonstrate how hydrological modifications create ecological traps through sublethal energetic costs, highlighting the need to maintain wetland connectivity and microtopographic complexity. Management strategies preserving minimum water depths >40 cm could mitigate these impacts across the species' Neotropical range.

We investigated the energetic consequences of coastal infrastructure development on Black-necked Stilts (Himantopus mexicanus) along the Upper Texas Coast from 2018-2020. Using miniaturized accelerometers (n=45 adults) paired with heart rate telemetry, we quantified daily energy expenditure (DEE) across three habitat types: natural salt marshes (n=15), managed wetlands (n=18), and construction-adjacent sites (n=12). Stilts in developed areas exhibited 22% higher DEE (mean ± SE: 153.2 ± 4.8 kJ/day) compared to natural sites (125.6 ± 3.1 kJ/day; linear mixed-effects model: β = 27.6, p<0.001), primarily due to increased flight frequency (3.2 vs. 1.4 flights/hr) and vigilance behavior. GPS tracking revealed developed site birds commuted 2.7 km farther daily to access foraging areas (Mann-Whitney U=23, p=0.008). Energy budgets showed construction-adjacent birds allocated 38% less time to foraging than natural site conspecifics, with corresponding 15% lower plasma triglyceride levels (t-test: t=3.41, p=0.002) indicating reduced energy acquisition. Despite elevated energy expenditure, nest success did not differ between sites (χ²=1.02, p=0.31), but post-fledging survival in developed areas was 19% lower (Kaplan-Meier log-rank test: χ²=5.62, p=0.02). Our results suggest coastal development imposes substantial metabolic costs through both increased energy output and constrained foraging opportunities, with latent effects manifesting in juvenile survival. These findings underscore the need for buffer zones around critical habitats and temporal restrictions on construction activities during breeding seasons to mitigate cumulative energetic impacts on shorebird populations.

We investigated microplastic transfer through predator-prey interactions in Purple Sandpipers (Calidris maritima) wintering in Svalbard, Norway (78°N), combining fecal analysis (n=120 individuals), prey sampling (n=450 Littorina saxatilis), and environmental microplastic surveys. Microplastics in bird feces (mean 12.3 ± 3.8 particles/g) showed strong correlation with concentrations in their principal gastropod prey (r=0.78, p<0.001), with polymer composition matching between trophic levels. Birds consuming >60% littorinids in their diet exhibited 2.3× higher microplastic loads than those relying on bivalves (GLM: β=1.42, SE=0.31, p=0.002). Juveniles showed 37% lower microplastic burdens than adults (t-test: t=3.21, p=0.004), potentially reflecting age-related foraging specialization. Sediment microplastic density (142-689 particles/kg) explained 64% of spatial variation in prey contamination (R²=0.64, p<0.001), with hotspots near glacier meltwater outflow zones increasing littorinid microplastics by 40% (ANOVA: F=8.9, p=0.016). Unexpectedly, 22% of microplastics exhibited biofilm colonization, suggesting potential trophic transfer of adhered contaminants. While no acute toxicity was observed (blood biochemistry p>0.05), long-term effects on nutrient assimilation require investigation. Results underscore the role of benthic food webs in microplastic propagation and highlight glacier-associated hydrodynamic processes as emerging contamination pathways in high-latitude shorebird habitats.

We investigated climate-mediated changes in egg characteristics and breeding success of Whimbrels (Numenius phaeopus) across a 37-year period (1985-2022) in the Yukon-Kuskokwim Delta, Alaska. Using historical museum collections (n=620 eggs) and contemporary field samples (n=580 eggs), we quantified temporal shifts in egg morphometrics, shell composition, and contaminant loads through vernier caliper measurements, atomic absorption spectroscopy, and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. Annual mean temperature increased 2.1°C (p<0.001) over the study period, with earlier spring thaw dates (β=-0.34 days/year, R²=0.41, p=0.002). Eggshell thickness decreased by 12% (2.14±0.11mm to 1.89±0.09mm, t=8.32, df=1198, p<0.001), approaching levels associated with DDT-era thinning, despite stable environmental pollutant concentrations (ΣPOPs=3.42±1.01ppm vs 3.39±1.12ppm). Counter to predictions, egg volume increased 8% (38.6±2.5cm³ to 41.7±3.1cm³, F=15.7, p<0.001), positively correlated with June temperatures (r=0.63, p=0.018). Hatching success declined from 72% to 58% (χ²=24.5, p<0.001), with precipitation variability explaining 34% of interannual variance (GLMM, z=-2.81, p=0.005). Mercury concentrations in eggshells exceeded toxicity thresholds in 18% of recent samples (0.52±0.21μg/g vs 0.49±0.19μg/g historically). Our results demonstrate complex climate impacts on Arctic-breeding shorebirds, revealing unexpected plastic responses in egg size but concerning declines in shell integrity and recruitment. These findings underscore the need for integrated contaminant monitoring and habitat protection across breeding and staging areas to buffer cascading climate effects on long-distance migrants.

We investigated the impacts of extreme weather events on Red-necked Phalarope (Phalaropus lobatus) demography using a 7-year dataset (2015-2022) from breeding grounds in the Yukon-Kuskokwim Delta, Alaska. Mark-recapture data (1,235 adults, 642 juveniles) combined with satellite telemetry (n=58) revealed significant age-specific survival responses to weather anomalies. Heatwave summers (≥3 consecutive days >21°C) reduced juvenile survival probability by 32% (95% CI: 21-42%) compared to average years, while adult survival remained high (0.89 ± 0.03 SE) across all conditions. Unseasonal snowstorms during early incubation (6 events in 2020-2022) caused 54% nest abandonment (n=217 nests), with renesting attempts showing 22% lower hatching success (χ²=7.41, p=0.006). Population matrix models incorporating NOAA climate data projected 17% decline in λ under RCP8.5 scenarios by 2040, primarily driven by reduced juvenile recruitment. Counterintuitively, adults exhibited behavioral flexibility with rapid (<48hr) relocation to ephemeral wetlands during drought years, as evidenced by GPS tracks (n=142 migrations). However, this plasticity did not buffer population-level effects, as demonstrated by a 41% decrease in colony size at long-term monitoring sites following consecutive extreme years (2018-2019). Our results highlight climate-driven demographic traps arising from age-specific vulnerabilities, emphasizing the need for habitat conservation targeting thermally buffered wetlands and storm-refugia areas. These findings underscore the importance of integrating extreme weather metrics into phalarope conservation planning across their Pacific Flyway range.

We investigated energy expenditure patterns of Wilson's Snipe (Gallinago delicata) across natural and converted salt marsh habitats in Louisiana's Mississippi River Delta using a combination of doubly labeled water measurements (n=42 adults) and GPS tracking. Birds in drained marshes converted to agricultural use exhibited 18% higher daily energy expenditure (DEE; 145.3 ± 8.7 kJ/day) compared to those in intact tidal marshes (122.9 ± 6.1 kJ/day; p<0.01) during winter months (November-February). This difference correlated with reduced invertebrate prey density (r²=0.63) and increased vigilance behavior linked to predator exposure in fragmented habitats. Plasma metabolite analysis revealed elevated triglyceride concentrations in converted marsh individuals (3.2 mmol/L vs 2.4 mmol/L), suggesting compensatory feeding strategies. However, converted marsh birds maintained 6.2% lower body mass (p=0.03) despite 31% longer daily foraging time (Mann-Whitney U=127, p=0.002). Spatial analysis showed 78% of tracked individuals (n=35) preferentially used remaining tidal channel networks, with 63% making daily movements >2 km to access freshwater seep zones. Our results demonstrate that marsh conversion disrupts energy budgets, though snipe demonstrate behavioral flexibility by exploiting transitional ecotones. Conservation efforts in critical wintering areas like Terrebonne and Plaquemines Parishes should prioritize maintaining tidal influence while creating freshwater foraging buffers adjacent to agricultural fields to mitigate energetic stressors.

Using satellite telemetry and field surveys, we investigated how intertidal shellfish harvesting impacts migration ecology in 48 Black-tailed Godwits (Limosa limosa limosa) along the East Atlantic Flyway from 2020–2023. GPS-tracked individuals (n=27 adults, 21 juveniles) showed significantly longer stopover durations (mean ± SE: 8.2 ± 1.3 days vs. 5.1 ± 0.9 days; p=0.017) and 32% reduced foraging efficiency at Mauritanian wintering sites with intensive Senilia senilis clam harvesting compared to protected areas. Benthic surveys revealed 41% lower macroinvertebrate biomass (ANOVA, F₁,₃₈=9.7, p=0.004) in harvested zones, correlating with godwits' increased daily energy expenditure (DLW method: 1,854 ± 214 kJ/day vs. 1,423 ± 189 kJ/day; t=3.11, p=0.003). Despite these constraints, survival rates (89% annual adult survival, MARK models) showed no significant decline, suggesting compensatory site-shifting behavior. However, juveniles in harvested areas exhibited 15% lower pre-migration body condition (mass/wing chord; t=2.34, p=0.023), potentially affecting subsequent breeding success. Stable isotope analysis (δ¹³C, δ¹⁵N) of blood samples indicated shifted dietary niches in exploited sites, with 28% higher reliance on polychaetes. Our results demonstrate that while adult godwits demonstrate behavioral plasticity to shellfishing pressure, chronic prey depletion may erode the quality of critical stopover habitats, particularly for inexperienced individuals. We recommend temporal harvesting closures during peak migration periods and buffer zones around key roost sites to maintain ecosystem services for migratory shorebirds.

We investigated the interacting effects of human disturbance and invasive plant encroachment on Wandering Tattler (Tringa incana) habitat use and behavior across 12 rocky intertidal sites in southeastern Alaska during 2019-2021 breeding seasons. Using 2,560 hours of behavioral observations from 45 tagged individuals combined with vegetation surveys, we quantified displacement responses to pedestrian activity (n=647 disturbance events) and measured Spartina alterniflora coverage in foraging areas. Mixed-effects models revealed a 32% reduction (β = -0.41, SE=0.12, p=0.003) in foraging time allocation within 50 m of trails experiencing >15 visitors/day. Radio-telemetry data showed 68% of individuals avoided invasive-dominated zones, with mean home range sizes 22% smaller (t=2.89, p=0.008) in invaded vs. native vegetation habitats. However, a Before-After Control-Impact experiment demonstrated 41% recovery of foraging efficiency following Spartina removal (F₁,₂₂=5.67, p=0.026), suggesting invasive management could partially mitigate habitat loss. Counterintuitively, disturbance frequency explained 18% more variance in baseline corticosterone levels (R²=0.29) than invasive plant coverage (R²=0.11), highlighting context-dependent stress responses. Our results indicate that while invasive species alter habitat structure, proximal anthropogenic disturbance remains the primary driver of behavioral modifications in this system. Conservation strategies require integrated approaches addressing both factors, particularly in high-use coastal recreation areas where these threats intersect.

We investigated population declines of Black-bellied Plovers (Pluvialis squatarola) in the eastern Canadian Arctic (Nunavut and Northwest Territories) from 2010-2022, focusing on interactions between coastal habitat degradation and traditional egg harvesting. Using drone surveys and nest monitoring across 12 breeding colonies (n=347 nests), we documented a 28% reduction in suitable nesting habitat (from 1,542 to 1,109 hectares) through satellite-based land cover analysis (Landsat 8, 30m resolution). Concurrently, egg collection pressure increased from 18% to 43% of nests affected per colony, based on community interviews and motion-activated camera data. Mixed-effects models revealed both factors significantly influenced reproductive success (habitat loss: β = -0.23, SE=0.07, p=0.001; egg collection: β = -0.17, SE=0.06, p=0.008), with synergistic effects reducing fledging rates by 62% in most degraded areas. Genetic analysis (microsatellite markers from 214 individuals) showed lower population connectivity (FST = 0.143) between colonies experiencing high anthropogenic pressure compared to undisturbed sites (FST = 0.072). However, community-led conservation initiatives implemented after 2018 in three colonies demonstrated 19% higher fledging success through rotational harvesting practices and predator exclusion fencing (χ²=4.31, df=1, p=0.038). Our results highlight the urgent need for integrated coastal zone management that balances traditional subsistence practices with plover conservation, particularly given accelerating Arctic shoreline erosion rates (2.3 m/year average retreat since 2015).

Recent range shifts in Black-necked Stilts (Himantopus mexicanus) along the Gulf of Mexico coast present novel interactions between climate change adaptation and anthropogenic pressures. Using 9 years of resighting data (2015-2023) from Texas to Veracruz, we quantified how hunting pressure modulates climate change impacts across 32 monitored populations (n = 2,374 banded individuals). Multistate mark-recapture models revealed hunting mortality rates increased from 11% to 22% in northern wintering areas following temperature anomalies exceeding 2°C above historic means (β = 0.47, 95% CI: 0.32-0.61). Coastal populations experiencing both intensive waterfowl hunting (≥5 hunters/km²) and habitat fragmentation showed 14% lower annual survival compared to protected estuaries (χ² = 18.3, p < 0.001), with juveniles disproportionately affected (mortality odds ratio = 3.1). Counterintuitively, telemetry data from 87 individuals revealed hunting grounds provided critical drought refugia, creating an ecological trap where stilt populations increased time-activity budgets by 38% in suboptimal habitats. Climate envelope projections incorporating current harvest rates predict 62% contraction of suitable wintering habitat by 2050 under RCP 6.0, compared to 41% contraction without hunting pressure. Our results demonstrate how localized harvest pressure amplifies climate-driven range shift constraints through demographic bottlenecks, highlighting the need for integrated adaptive management that addresses both thermodynamic thresholds and harvest dynamics in coastal wetland ecosystems.

We investigated breeding habitat selection by Long-billed Curlews (Numenius americanus) across a gradient of coastal development in Padilla Bay, Washington, from 2018-2020. Using GPS telemetry (n=38 adults) coupled with high-resolution land cover classification, we assessed resource selection through generalized linear mixed models incorporating individual random effects. Curlews exhibited strong selection for tidal flats (β=1.32±0.41 SE, p<0.001) and fallow agricultural fields (β=0.87±0.33, p=0.008) while avoiding urbanized areas (β=-2.15±0.62, p<0.001) at the 50-ha scale. At finer scales (5-ha), nest site selection correlated with visual obscurity (≥40 cm vegetation height: odds ratio=3.2, 95% CI=1.8-5.7) and absence of human structures within 500 m (odds ratio=4.1, 2.3-7.4). Nest success declined by 22% (95% CI=14-29%) for each 1.5 km decrease in distance to coastal development, primarily due to increased predation rates in fragmented habitats (R²=0.47). However, wintering adults demonstrated behavioral plasticity, utilizing modified habitats including managed wetlands (27% of locations) and pasturelands (19%) when tidal resources were limited. Population viability analysis indicated that maintaining ≥60% undisturbed habitat within 2 km of nesting areas could support λ≥1.0 despite projected sea-level rise scenarios. Our results highlight the importance of implementing development setback buffers while maintaining heterogeneous habitat mosaics to accommodate both breeding and wintering phase requirements in rapidly developing coastal ecosystems.

We investigated Western Sandpiper (Calidris mauri) habitat selection in response to coastal mudflat reclamation across 23 sites in the Yellow Sea's Bohai Bay, China, during 2018–2020 migration seasons. Using GPS telemetry (n = 48 adults) paired with invertebrate sampling and tidal hydrology data, we compared resource selection between natural intertidal flats and adjacent reclaimed areas (seawall-constrained aquaculture ponds and saltworks). Generalized linear mixed models revealed strong avoidance of reclaimed habitats (β = -1.62, 95% CI: -2.31–-0.93, p < 0.001), with individuals using these areas 78% less frequently than expected based on availability. Foraging rates in reclaimed zones averaged 0.3 ± 0.1 prey items/min versus 1.2 ± 0.3 in natural habitats (t = 4.71, p < 0.001). Population surveys showed a 34% decline in local sandpiper abundance (95% CI: 28–40%) over five years in heavily reclaimed regions, compared to stable trends in less-modified areas. However, remnant natural patches >2 ha within reclaimed landscapes hosted 12% higher densities (95% CI: 5–19%) than continuous habitats, suggesting threshold-dependent utility. Contrary to expectations, nocturnal roost site selection showed no significant difference between habitat types (p = 0.18). Our findings highlight the acute sensitivity of migratory shorebirds to tidal flat loss, with population-level impacts mediated by both habitat area reduction and fragmentation effects. Conservation strategies prioritizing retention of natural sediment dynamics and connectivity between remnant patches could mitigate demographic consequences for this declining species.

Long-term demographic monitoring of Lesser Yellowlegs (*Tringa flavipes*) across North American breeding and wintering grounds (2010-2025; n = 2,514 individuals) revealed hunting pressure disproportionately impacts adult survival during migration. Using Cormack-Jolly-Seber models with banding-recovery data from 23 sites and satellite telemetry (n = 87 adults), we quantified survival probabilities across hunting and non-hunting zones. Adult annual survival averaged 0.72 (95% CI: 0.68-0.76) in regions with regulated harvests versus 0.64 (0.59-0.69) in high-hunting areas (ΔAICc = 12.7, p < 0.001), with strongest effects during autumn migration in the Mississippi Flyway. Juvenile survival (0.65 ± 0.04 SE) showed no direct hunting association but correlated with wetland habitat availability (β = 0.22, p = 0.03). Integrated population models indicated regional declines of 2.8% annually in hunted populations versus stable trends (-0.1% ± 1.3%) in protected regions, despite comparable breeding productivity (1.2 fledglings/pair). Counterintuitively, hunting mortality showed density-dependent compensation in Alberta breeding populations (R² = 0.41), where higher predation rates buffered additive harvest effects. These results contrast with Caribbean wintering populations exhibiting hunting-driven declines (λ = 0.92) without compensatory mechanisms. Our continental-scale analysis identifies critical thresholds (≤15% annual adult mortality from hunting) to maintain population stability, emphasizing the need for adaptive harvest management coordinated across flyways. Conservation prioritization should address regional disparities, particularly in Maranhão, Brazil, where unregulated hunting coincides with mangrove habitat loss.

We examined how recreational egg collection influences habitat selection and reproductive strategies in Common Sandpipers (Actitis hypoleucos) across the Brahmaputra River floodplain, Assam, India, during 2020-2021 breeding seasons. Using radio-telemetry (n=64 adults) and nest monitoring (34 egg-collected vs 30 control nests), we quantified nest-site characteristics and re-nesting behavior following egg removal. Nests subjected to collection were 23% more likely to occur in dense riverside vegetation (OR=1.74, 95% CI:1.12-2.71) compared to undisturbed nests, suggesting selection for visual concealment. However, re-nesting attempts after egg collection showed reduced habitat selectivity, with 41% of pairs utilizing suboptimal open gravel bars. Survival analysis revealed significantly lower daily nest survival rates in re-nesting attempts (0.932 ± 0.017 SE) versus initial nests (0.966 ± 0.011 SE), with human disturbance proximity explaining 68% of failure risk (hazard ratio=2.3). Adults from collected nests exhibited 52% greater post-disturbance movement distances (mean=1.2 km vs 0.8 km controls, p<0.001), incurring measurable energetic costs (7.8% higher plasma corticosterone). While population modeling indicated current collection rates (<15% nests/year) permit regional persistence (λ=0.986), projected increases to 25% collection risk would drive 14% annual declines. These results demonstrate adaptive but energetically costly habitat selection responses to non-lethal human disturbance, highlighting the need for spatially explicit management of riparian zones to maintain heterogeneous vegetation structure while regulating localized collection pressures.

We investigated the impacts of recreational disturbance on Piping Plover (Charadrius melodus) habitat use and reproductive success across 12 managed coastal wetlands in the Great Lakes region from 2018-2020. Using GPS tracking (n=45 adults) and nest monitoring (n=120 nests), we quantified spatial overlap between human activities and plover resource selection. Plovers showed significant avoidance zones extending 150 m from pedestrian trails (mixed-effects models, β = -1.32 ± 0.41 SE, p<0.001) and 220 m from off-leash dog zones (β = -2.01 ± 0.38, p<0.001). Nest survival probability decreased by 42% when human disturbance events occurred within 50 m during incubation (daily survival rate 0.963 vs 0.914, χ²=7.3, p=0.007). However, beaches implementing dawn-to-10am closures during peak hatchling rearing (June 15-July 30) showed 28% higher fledging success (1.42 chicks/pair) compared to unrestricted sites (1.11 chicks/pair, t-test p=0.03). Counterintuitively, regulated wrack removal reduced chick foraging habitat quality more significantly than recreational impacts at three sites (invertebrate biomass 23% lower in managed zones, ANOVA p=0.012). Our multi-scale analysis revealed spatial thresholds where managed access (≤12 visitors/hr within 300m of nesting areas) maintained both recreational use and plover productivity. These findings highlight the necessity of dynamic, habitat-specific management strategies that balance human activity with critical life-stage requirements for this threatened shorebird.

We investigated the impacts of invasive common reed (Phragmites australis) encroachment on Solitary Sandpiper (Tringa solitaria) migration ecology in the Saskatchewan River Delta, Canada, from 2018-2021. Using light-level geolocators deployed on 45 adults across three breeding seasons, we found that individuals from territories with >40% Phragmites coverage exhibited 18% later autumn departure dates (ANCOVA: F₁,₃₈=7.2, p=0.011) and 22% shorter migration distances (mean ± SD: 4,320 ± 610 km vs 5,540 ± 890 km) compared to those from native cattail-dominated habitats. Radio-telemetry data from 127 tracked juveniles revealed significantly lower fledging success in invaded areas (0.78 chicks/pair vs 1.24 in native habitats; t-test: t=3.41, p<0.001). Stable isotope analysis of 234 feather samples indicated reduced aquatic invertebrate consumption in Phragmites sites (δ¹⁵N values 8.7‰ vs 11.2‰, PERMANOVA: F=14.3, p=0.002), correlating with lower pre-migration body condition (r=-0.34, p=0.017). Despite these fitness consequences, occupancy modeling using 1,234 survey points showed a 13% annual range shift into disturbed wetlands, suggesting ecological traps may be forming. Our findings highlight the need for active Phragmites management in critical stopover habitats, particularly along the western flyway where 68% of monitored sites showed invasive expansion exceeding 5%/year. These results underscore the species' adaptive challenges in rapidly changing wetland ecosystems.

We investigated the impacts of legacy and emerging contaminants on Red Knot (Calidris canutus rufa) breeding biology at a key Arctic nesting site in southwest Greenland (67°N) from 2018-2022. Blood samples from 85 adults and 320 eggs were analyzed for mercury (Hg), perfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), and polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) via LC-MS/MS, alongside endocrine profiling (corticosterone, prolactin). Contaminant concentrations showed strong bioaccumulation patterns, with adults exhibiting Hg levels (2.1 ± 0.7 ppm ww) exceeding toxicity thresholds in 38% of individuals. Eggs from nests of high-Hg females (>2.1 ppm) showed 34% lower hatching success (β = -0.41, SE = 0.12, p = 0.002) and 22% longer incubation periods compared to low-Hg pairs (<1.0 ppm). PCB concentrations in adult plasma (ΣPCBs 6.8 ± 2.3 ng/g ww) correlated with suppressed prolactin levels (r = -0.47, p = 0.008), potentially disrupting parental care behaviors. While PFAS exposure (ΣPFAS 34.5 ± 11.2 ng/g ww) showed no direct effects on embryonic development, chick growth rates declined by 15% in nests where both parents exhibited combined contaminant loads above the 75th percentile (F₁,₆₂ = 5.11, p = 0.027). Our findings demonstrate contaminant-mediated fitness costs across multiple breeding stages, with Hg and PCBs posing particular risks to this declining subspecies. These results underscore the need for pan-Arctic pollutant monitoring in shorebird conservation strategies, as bioaccumulated chemicals may compound existing threats from climate change and habitat loss.

We investigated nest site selection and trampling vulnerability in Black Oystercatchers (Haematopus bachmani) across 23 islands in British Columbia, Canada, during 2021–2022 breeding seasons. Using GPS mapping of 127 nests paired with motion-activated camera traps, we quantified microhabitat characteristics and documented 284 trampling events by mammals (68%) and humans (32%). Logistic regression models revealed nests in elevations <3.2 m above mean high water (OR = 4.7, 95% CI: 2.1–10.3, p<0.01) and <15 m from the high tide line (OR = 3.1, 95% CI: 1.7–5.6) faced significantly higher trampling risk, while vegetative cover (measured through 1-m² quadrats) showed no significant association. Nest survival analysis using the Shaffer method demonstrated daily survival rates 22% lower in high-trampling zones (0.963 vs. 0.985). However, 41% of pairs selected historically trampled areas for re-nesting attempts, with no significant difference in clutch size between high-risk and low-risk sites (Mann-Whitney U=1894, p=0.34). Population viability analysis suggested chronic trampling could reduce local productivity by 18–34%, with 34% of trampling-induced failures resulting in complete breeding abandonment. Our results indicate adaptive nest site selection maintains demographic resilience despite frequent disturbance, but emphasize the need for managed access to low-elevation gravel beaches during peak incubation (May–July). These findings challenge assumptions about passive habitat selection in intertidal specialists and highlight elevation thresholds as critical parameters for shoreline management plans.

We investigated interactive effects of introduced mammalian predators and heavy metal contamination on Killdeer (Charadrius vociferus) reproductive success across 15 breeding sites in coastal British Columbia, Canada, from 2019-2021. Using motion-activated cameras and weekly nest monitoring (n = 300 nests), we documented a 45% nest failure rate attributed primarily to raccoon (Procyon lotor) and feral cat (Felis catus) predation, with predation risk 2.8 times higher (95% CI: 1.9-4.1) in urban-adjacent habitats versus protected areas. Eggshell analysis revealed significantly higher lead (2.3 ± 0.7 ppm vs. 0.9 ± 0.3 ppm; t = 4.12, p < 0.001) and cadmium concentrations (0.4 ± 0.1 ppm vs. 0.2 ± 0.05 ppm) in abandoned nests compared to successful clutches, suggesting predator-induced stress may exacerbate pollutant bioaccumulation. Nest abandonment probability increased nonlinearly with both predator encounter frequency (R² = 0.67) and hepatic metal loads in adult females (R² = 0.52), with synergistic effects explaining 38% of variance in clutch failure. However, blood metallothionein levels showed no significant relationship with predation pressure (F₁,₁₂₈ = 1.23, p = 0.27), indicating potential threshold effects in detoxification capacity. Our results demonstrate that anthropogenic predators mediate pollution impacts through behavioral and physiological pathways, with abandoned nests containing 18% higher contaminant loads than depredated ones (χ² = 7.89, p = 0.005). These findings emphasize the need for integrated management of invasive species and pollution mitigation in shorebird conservation planning.

We investigated heavy metal accumulation in Kentish Plovers across a human disturbance gradient along the South China coast during 2019–2022 breeding seasons. Using non-invasive eggshell sampling (n = 120 nests) and blood plasma analysis from 78 adults, we quantified lead (Pb), mercury (Hg), and cadmium (Cd) concentrations via ICP-MS. Nest sites within 500m of tourist facilities (n = 42) showed 38% higher Pb levels (mean ± SE: 2.74 ± 0.21 μg/g vs. 1.98 ± 0.15 μg/g; p = 0.003) and 27% elevated Hg compared to undisturbed sites. Daily visitor counts (range: 15–420 individuals/day) positively correlated with Pb contamination (β = 0.42, R² = 0.31, p < 0.01). Controlled incubation experiments revealed Pb concentrations >3.2 μg/g reduced hatching success by 41% (OR = 2.3, 95% CI: 1.4–3.8). However, Cd showed no significant bioaccumulation pattern (p = 0.17) despite comparable environmental exposure. Chromium levels remained below detection limits (<0.05 μg/g) across all sites. Adults from high-disturbance areas exhibited altered foraging rhythms, with 22% less time spent feeding during peak tourist hours (10:00–14:00). Our results demonstrate differential metal accumulation patterns influenced by anthropogenic activity intensity, suggesting plovers may serve as bioindicators for coastal pollution monitoring. Management strategies should prioritize buffer zone establishment around critical nesting habitats and regulate vehicular access during sensitive breeding phases.

We investigated the role of vocalizations in mediating competitive exclusion between Wilson's Plovers (Charadrius wilsonia) and sympatric shorebirds along the Gulf Coast of Florida, USA, during the 2021-2023 breeding seasons. Using bioacoustic recordings (n = 1,742 calls from 126 individuals) synchronized with 480 hours of behavioral observations, we quantified territorial call parameters and interspecific responses. Wilson's Plovers produced aggressive calls at lower frequencies (2.1 ± 0.4 kHz vs. 3.5 ± 0.6 kHz in Snowy Plovers, Charadrius nivosus) and higher amplitudes (86.2 ± 3.1 dB vs. 78.9 ± 4.2 dB) during boundary disputes. Playback experiments revealed 73% of competing species (7/10) altered space use following Wilson's Plover vocalizations, with Snowy Plovers showing 42% greater nest site displacement (95% CI: 33-51%) than controls. However, no avoidance responses occurred from larger species like Black Skimmers (Rynchops niger). Acoustic niche analysis demonstrated significant spectral overlap with two smaller plover species (Bhattacharyya coefficient >0.7, p<0.01), suggesting vocal interference potential. Mixed-effects models identified call rate (β = -0.87, SE = 0.21, p<0.001) rather than frequency as the primary predictor of competitor displacement. These findings reveal asymmetric acoustic competition mediating habitat segregation in mixed shorebird communities, with implications for managing coastal habitats to maintain acoustic refugia for subordinate competitors.

We investigated plastic pollution impacts on Wilson's Snipe (Gallinago delicata) through necropsies of 142 individuals collected from southern Lake Michigan wetlands during 2019-2021 spring migrations. Using FTIR spectroscopy and body condition metrics, we quantified plastic ingestion and associated health effects. Sixty-seven percent of specimens contained plastics (mean 12.3 ± 4.7 particles/individual), predominantly microplastics (<5mm) composed of polyethylene (58%) and polypropylene (27%). Birds with plastic loads exceeding 15 particles showed significantly lower body mass (β = -0.18, p = 0.003) and reduced hepatic fat reserves (F₁,₁₃₈ = 9.41, p = 0.003) compared to less contaminated individuals. Juveniles exhibited higher plastic ingestion rates than adults (χ² = 6.24, p = 0.012), with 83% of first-year birds containing plastics versus 57% of adults. Seasonal patterns revealed 32% higher plastic loads during early migration compared to peak staging periods. Contrary to expectations, metal concentrations (Pb, Cd, Hg) showed no correlation with plastic burdens (all p > 0.05). Gut microbiome analysis of 30 individuals demonstrated altered microbial diversity in high-plastic specimens (Shannon index Δ = 0.87, p = 0.021), particularly reductions in cellulose-digesting bacteria. Our results identify agricultural runoff and degraded urban debris as primary plastic sources, with wetland sediments containing 2,143 ± 892 particles/kg dry weight. These findings highlight previously undocumented sublethal effects of plastic pollution on a cryptic shorebird species, emphasizing the role of freshwater wetlands as microplastic sinks impacting specialized probe-foraging birds.

We investigated the impacts of altered storm regimes on the energy budgets of Kentish Plovers (Charadrius alexandrinus) across six Mediterranean breeding sites (Tunisia, 2020-2023) using a combination of accelerometry (n=48 adults), heart rate telemetry, and microclimate modeling. During 137 storm events (wind speeds >14 m/s, precipitation >20 mm/day), plovers exhibited 18% higher resting metabolic rates (RMR) compared to baseline conditions (p<0.001, R²=0.47), with energy expenditure increasing exponentially at wind chill temperatures below 5°C. GPS tracking revealed storm-induced habitat shifts increased daily movement distances by 1.7±0.3 km (p=0.002), while time allocated to foraging decreased by 32% during prolonged storms (>6 hours). Chick-rearing adults showed particularly pronounced effects, with mean daily energy expenditure 22% higher than non-breeding birds during storms (p=0.013). Analysis of 412 prey samples demonstrated storm-related reductions in polychaete worm availability (prey density decrease of 47±12%), forcing plovers to switch to less energetically favorable amphipods. Population-level consequences emerged through a 41% reduction in chick survival rates (n=127 broods) following spring storms, mediated through both thermoregulatory costs and reduced provisioning rates. Our models predict current storm intensification trends could increase adult overwinter mortality by 14-19% in migratory populations, but resident populations showed higher resilience (7% predicted increase). These results highlight climate-driven energetic bottlenecks during critical life stages, emphasizing the need for dynamic habitat management that preserves sheltered foraging areas adjacent to breeding zones.

We investigated how coastal infrastructure development modulates disturbance regimes for Ruddy Turnstones (Arenaria interpres) at Delaware Bay, a critical spring stopover site, during 2021-2022 migratory seasons. Using standardized behavioral scans (n = 980 observation periods) and GPS tracking of 42 individuals equipped with VHF transmitters, we quantified anthropogenic interactions across 15 beaches spanning undeveloped to highly modified shorelines. Mixed-effects models revealed that hourly pedestrian frequency exceeding 23 persons/km (β = 0.17, SE = 0.04, p < 0.001) and construction activity within 300 m of the high-tide line (β = -0.29, SE = 0.11, p = 0.009) reduced mean foraging time by 38% compared to protected areas. Flight initiation distances decreased by 22% at developed sites (F₁₃,₈₆ = 4.71, p = 0.03), suggesting partial habitation, but peck rates remained 18% lower (95% CI: 7-29%) despite available prey. Developed areas showed 45% shorter residency periods (median 2.3 vs. 4.1 days) and 310 g lower mean departure mass (t₃₈ = 2.96, p = 0.005), potentially compromising transatlantic flights. However, turnover rates increased at modified sites (Mantel test r = 0.41, p = 0.02), indicating compensatory redistribution. Our findings highlight spatial thresholds where cumulative disturbance exceeds species' adjustment capacity, particularly during peak horseshoe crab spawning (May 20-June 5). Managed retreat of recreational infrastructure and temporal activity restrictions during mass feeding periods could enhance refueling efficiency at this internationally significant stopover.

We investigated the effects of anthropogenic noise on Whimbrel (Numenius phaeopus) behavior and interspecific interactions at six critical migration stopover sites in the Wadden Sea, Germany, during spring migration (March–May 2022). Using acoustic recorders and behavioral scans (n = 1,240 observation periods), we quantified noise levels (dB(A)) and compared foraging rates, vigilance behavior, and shorebird community composition across low-noise (<50 dB) and high-noise (>65 dB) zones. Whimbrels in high-noise areas exhibited 32% lower prey capture rates (p = 0.004) and 1.7 times more frequent vigilance behavior (p = 0.01) compared to conspecifics in quieter zones. Noise levels exceeding 60 dB correlated with a 41% reduction in co-occurring shorebird species richness (R² = 0.63, p < 0.001), though prey availability (polychaete density) showed no significant difference between zones (t-test, p = 0.22). Fecal glucocorticoid metabolite analysis (n = 78 samples) revealed 28% higher stress hormone concentrations in high-noise sites (p = 0.03). However, telemetry data from 22 GPS-tagged individuals showed no significant avoidance of noisy areas during stopover site selection. Our results suggest noise pollution imposes physiological costs and alters fine-scale habitat use patterns, potentially disrupting community dynamics at critical migration stages. These findings support targeted noise mitigation in coastal reserves during peak migration periods, though the lack of large-scale avoidance behavior underscores the need for comprehensive habitat protection strategies.

This study investigates the compounding effects of nest trampling and climate change on Northern Jacana (Jacana spinosa) reproductive success across 12 wetland sites in central Panama from 2018–2022. Using 347 nest observations tracked via daily camera traps and environmental sensors, we quantified trampling frequency from livestock and ecotourism activities, while monitoring microhabitat changes linked to precipitation anomalies (mean +23% wet season rainfall vs. 30-year baseline). Multivariate logistic regression revealed trampling caused 35% of nest failures (n=121), disproportionately affecting early incubation stages (OR=2.7, 95% CI:1.8–4.1). Nest sites with >15 cm water depth fluctuations showed 58% higher trampling probability (χ²=9.34, p=0.002) as shifting hydrology compressed suitable nesting areas. Counterintuitively, trampling mortality decreased by 41% in marshes with intact shoreline vegetation (>80% cover), suggesting buffering capacity against both physical disturbance and thermal stress (mean nest temperatures 2.3°C cooler). Climate projections indicate trampling impacts could increase 3-fold by 2050 under RCP6.0 due to synergistic effects of habitat fragmentation and extreme rainfall events. However, adaptive management trials demonstrated rotating livestock exclusion periods during peak incubation months improved fledging success by 22% without affecting pastoral livelihoods. Results highlight the necessity of integrated wetland management strategies addressing both anthropogenic pressures and hydrological changes to enhance resilience in this climate-vulnerable shorebird species.

We investigated the effects of recreational photography pressure on Black-bellied Plover (Pluvialis squatarola) populations across 12 coastal sites in the Wadden Sea World Heritage Site from 2018-2020. Using a combination of focal animal sampling (n = 75 tagged individuals) and visitor behavior surveys (n = 320 observation hours), we quantified disturbance frequency and duration during both spring (n = 142 events) and fall migration (n = 189 events). Plovers exposed to photographer approaches within 50 m showed a 23% reduction in foraging time (GLMM: β = -0.41 ± 0.09 SE, p < 0.001) and 17% higher vigilance rates compared to control sites (χ² = 9.32, p = 0.002). Time-exposure models revealed cumulative disturbance effects, with individuals experiencing >3 photographer interactions/hour exhibiting 12% lower body condition indices (ANCOVA: F₁,₇₂ = 6.85, p = 0.011). Population viability analysis incorporating these behavioral impacts predicted a 14% decline in local plover numbers over 10 years under current disturbance levels. However, experimental implementation of 150-m buffer zones during critical feeding periods (1 hour before/after high tide) reduced disturbance frequency by 68% (Mann-Whitney U = 41, p < 0.001) without affecting photographer satisfaction (survey β = 0.12 ± 0.21 SE, p = 0.57). Our results demonstrate that unregulated coastal photography creates ecological traps for staging plovers, but spatially explicit management can mitigate these impacts while maintaining human access. Long-term monitoring showed no carryover effects on subsequent breeding success in Arctic nesting populations (logistic regression: OR = 1.04, 95% CI 0.92-1.17), suggesting acute migratory-phase impacts rather than chronic population-level consequences.

We investigated the impacts of ocean acidification on American Golden-Plover (Pluvialis dominica) populations across their Pacific flyway migration route from 2010-2022. Using a combination of mark-recapture data (n = 2,347 individuals), satellite telemetry, and carbonate chemistry monitoring, we assessed breeding success, juvenile survival, and adult body condition in relation to aragonite saturation states (Ωarag) at key coastal stopover sites. Our analysis revealed significant spatial variation in acidification exposure, with birds utilizing the East Asian-Australasian Flyway experiencing 27% lower mean Ωarag levels (1.2 ± 0.3) compared to those using the Americas Flyway (1.7 ± 0.4). Population models incorporating decadal pH trends showed a 15% reduction in lifetime reproductive success for cohorts exposed to Ωarag <1.5 during critical spring staging periods. Counterintuitively, adult survival rates increased by 8% in moderately acidified regions (Ωarag 1.3-1.5), potentially due to prey concentration effects, while crashing at Ωarag <1.1. Isotopic analysis of blood samples (n = 892) indicated a 40% reduction in polychaete consumption - a key calcium source - in acidified areas, correlating with thinner eggshells (14% reduction, p=0.032) at Arctic breeding colonies. Our findings suggest non-linear population responses to acidification, with current levels already impacting recruitment in 38% of the studied populations. These results emphasize the need for integrated marine-terrestrial conservation strategies, particularly for intertidal habitats in the Yellow Sea and Gulf of Alaska where acidification thresholds approach critical biological limits.

We investigated the impacts of microplastic contamination on foraging ecology and predation risk in Ruddy Turnstones (Arenaria interpres) across three major migratory stopover sites in the Wadden Sea (2019-2021). Using a combination of GPS tracking (n=48 adults), prey item analysis (1,237 identified food objects), and fecal microplastic quantification, we found 92% of individuals contained ingested microplastics (mean 14.6±3.2 particles/g feces). Turnstones consuming >10 microplastic particles/g showed 23% lower mean hourly prey intake rates (GLMM: β=-0.41, SE=0.12, p=0.003) and spent 37% more time vigilant compared to less contaminated conspecifics. Plastic-laden birds exhibited significant prey selectivity shifts, with a 15% reduction in preferred hard-shelled mollusk consumption and increased reliance on softer polychaetes (χ²=8.91, df=2, p=0.012). Paradoxically, high microplastic burdens correlated with 28% lower fox predation rates (Cox PH model: HR=0.72, 95% CI 0.61-0.85), potentially due to altered activity patterns reducing detectability. Juveniles carried 41% higher microplastic loads than adults (Welch's t=3.78, p<0.001), suggesting age-dependent exposure risks. Our results demonstrate complex cascading effects where microplastics alter predator-prey dynamics through both physiological impacts on foraging efficiency and unexpected behavioral-mediated predation outcomes, highlighting the need for integrated plastic pollution monitoring in coastal conservation strategies.

We investigated phenological mismatches in Wattled Jacana (Jacana jacana) breeding ecology using stable isotope analysis (δ13C, δ15N) across 12 wetland complexes in the Orinoco Basin, Colombia, during 2018-2021. Blood samples from 236 adults and 127 chicks were compared with isotopic baselines from aquatic invertebrate prey populations sampled weekly throughout three annual cycles. Bayesian mixing models revealed a critical 17.3 ± 2.1 day advancement in peak availability of Armored Catfish (Callichthyidae) eggs, a key protein source for chick-rearing adults, while jacana nest initiation dates showed only 6.4 ± 1.8 day advancement (mixed-effects model: F3,412 = 18.9, p < 0.001). This trophic decoupling resulted in 34% lower chick survival rates (n = 89 broods) when hatch dates fell >10 days post-prey peak, compared to matched pairs (Cox proportional hazard ratio = 2.17, 95% CI 1.45-3.24). Feather δ15N values from surviving juveniles (n = 47) were 1.8‰ higher than non-survivors (n = 112; t-test: t157 = 3.11, p = 0.002), indicating dietary plasticity mediates mismatch impacts. However, only 29% of adults shifted to alternative prey during mismatched years, with wetland fragmentation severity explaining 61% of variance in prey-switching capacity (GLM: β = -0.83 ± 0.19 SE). Results demonstrate climate-driven phenological shifts disrupt critical trophic linkages, emphasizing the need for dynamic wetland management that maintains diverse invertebrate communities to buffer mismatches.

We investigated the interactive effects of coastal habitat degradation and heavy metal exposure on Pied Avocet (Recurvirostra avosetta) populations across 12 estuaries in the East Atlantic Flyway (52°N-21°N) from 2018-2022. Using a combination of sediment analysis (n=480 samples), blood metal concentrations (120 adults, 60 chicks), and GPS tracking data (45 individuals), we quantified spatial overlap between tidal flat loss (18.7% reduction in core foraging areas since 2000) and zinc, cadmium, and lead contamination hotspots. Adults in degraded habitats showed 34% higher blood cadmium concentrations (mean=2.1 μg/g dw vs 1.4 μg/g in intact sites; p=0.013) and significantly reduced body condition indices (BCI=-0.28±0.12 SE). Chick survival probabilities decreased by 22% in areas combining >30% habitat loss with metal levels exceeding sediment quality guidelines (χ²=6.84, p=0.032). Isotopic mixing models revealed increased reliance on metal-contaminated polychaete prey (δ¹³C analysis) in altered estuaries. However, population viability analysis indicated compensatory mechanisms, with juveniles from contaminated sites exhibiting 41% greater dispersal distances (median=127 km vs 74 km). Our results demonstrate habitat fragmentation amplifies metal exposure risks through both geochemical concentration processes and constrained foraging strategies, though metallothionein induction levels (1.7-3.2 nmol/g) suggest sub-lethal rather than acute toxicity. These findings underscore the need for integrated coastal zone management addressing both physical habitat loss and chemical pollution to protect avocet populations along anthropogenic coastlines.

We investigated population dynamics of Short-billed Dowitchers (Limnodromus griseus griseus) in the Delaware Bay stopover region (New Jersey, USA) from 2015-2020 to assess responses to interannual variation in benthic prey availability. Using mark-recapture data (n=2,347 individuals) coupled with systematic prey sampling (sediment cores to 15 cm depth), we quantified relationships between horseshoe crab (Limulus polyphemus) egg density, polychaete (Alitta succinea) biomass, and shorebird survival probabilities. Bayesian hierarchical models revealed strong non-linear responses: adult daily survival probability increased from 0.972 (95% CI: 0.961-0.980) at low prey densities (<5,000 eggs/m²) to 0.991 (0.985-0.995) above 15,000 eggs/m². Juvenile survival showed greater sensitivity to polychaete availability (β=0.43 ±0.11 SE per log(biomass)). Population matrix projections indicated a 22% decline in local stopover populations when crab egg densities fell below 10,000 eggs/m² for consecutive years, though fecundity estimates from 137 tracked breeders showed no significant relationship with wintering ground prey conditions (p=0.21). Temporal offset analysis revealed a 9-day advancement in peak migration timing (R²=0.67) correlated with earlier spring water temperature maxima. Our results demonstrate age-specific vulnerability to resource fluctuations and suggest carryover effects from migration resource bottlenecks may disproportionately impact juvenile recruitment. These findings underscore the importance of maintaining threshold prey densities at key stopover sites through combined habitat protection and dynamic resource monitoring programs.

We conducted a 12-year demographic study (2008-2020) of Wattled Jacana populations in the seasonally flooded grasslands of Venezuela's Llanos region to quantify impacts of wetland drainage for agriculture. Using mark-recapture data from 1,234 adults and nest monitoring of 2,897 breeding attempts, we compared survival probabilities and reproductive success across intact wetlands (n=6 sites) versus drained areas (n=4). Bayesian survival analysis revealed significantly lower annual adult survival in drained habitats (φ=0.62 ± 0.04 SE) compared to natural wetlands (φ=0.78 ± 0.03). Nest success showed stronger declines, with only 18.7% of clutches reaching hatching in drained sites versus 35.9% in intact wetlands (OR=0.52, 95%CI=0.41-0.66). Despite similar clutch sizes (x̄=3.8 eggs vs 3.7), drained areas exhibited higher chick mortality from desiccation (62% mortality before fledging vs 41%). Matrix population models projected an 8.2% annual decline in drained sites versus stable populations (-0.3%) in natural wetlands. Genetic analysis of 147 individuals revealed 32% lower allelic richness in fragmented populations (F<sub>IS</sub>=0.18 vs 0.09). Our results demonstrate wetland drainage creates dual demographic bottlenecks by reducing both adult survival and recruitment. Conservation efforts must prioritize maintaining natural hydrologic regimes, as drained habitats cannot maintain source populations despite high initial breeding densities. Urgent action is needed to protect remaining floodplain complexes, with at least 30% wetland coverage required to maintain population viability.

We investigated how wetland management practices influence phenological mismatches in Ruddy Turnstones (Arenaria interpres) across six managed wetlands in the Delaware Bay, USA, during spring migration (2018–2020). Using a combination of GPS telemetry (n = 75 individuals), weekly invertebrate sampling, and water level records, we quantified mismatches between peak prey abundance (predominantly limnephilid caddisfly larvae) and shorebird arrival timing. Managed wetlands experienced delayed prey emergence (mean ± SD: 12.3 ± 3.7 days later) compared to natural reference sites following spring drawdowns. Turnstones arriving during early migration phases (days 120–135 since January 1) exhibited 23% lower foraging success rates (GLMM: β = -0.41, SE = 0.12, p < 0.001) and 15% lower mass gain (linear mixed model: F₁,₂₃₈ = 18.9, p < 0.001) at managed sites versus natural wetlands. Hydrological modeling revealed that drawdown initiation dates preceding bird arrival by <7 days exacerbated resource mismatches (R² = 0.68 for prey biomass prediction). However, two wetlands implementing adaptive drawdowns synchronized with real-time migration tracking via Motus stations showed no significant mismatch effects (t-test: t = 1.12, p = 0.27). Our results demonstrate that current water management protocols developed for waterfowl inadvertently create trophic mismatches for migratory shorebirds, reducing refueling efficiency by 18–32% at critical staging sites. We propose a dynamic management framework incorporating shorebird migration forecasts and phased drawdowns to align wetland productivity peaks with stopover phenology, potentially increasing seasonal survival rates by 9–14% for this declining species.

We investigated the impacts of accelerated sea level rise on Wilson's Phalarope (Phalaropus tricolor) populations in the Great Salt Lake ecosystem from 2015-2022 using mark-recapture (n=1,200 adults) and nest monitoring data (n=350 nests). Bayesian integrated population models revealed differential impacts across life stages, with adult survival probability (Φ=0.78±0.04 SE) remaining stable despite a 19% reduction in preferred hypersaline habitat. However, nest success declined by 32% (β=-0.41±0.11, 95% CrI[-0.63,-0.19]) as rising lake levels increased nest flooding frequency (r=-0.83 between water level and nest survival). Chick survival showed threshold responses to prey availability, declining sharply when salinity exceeded 12% (Hazard Ratio=2.7, p<0.001). Population viability analysis projected a 45% decline by 2040 under current inundation rates (R²=0.91 with observed counts), but highlighted resilience through juvenile recruitment plasticity (λ=1.12 when first-year survival >0.31). Spatial analysis identified critical vulnerability in northern wetland complexes (87% of successful nests) where vegetation loss rates exceeded 5%/year. Our results demonstrate that while adults exhibit strong site fidelity to suboptimal habitats, the species' future depends on maintaining hydrological refugia with salinity gradients >8-15% during breeding. Conservation strategies must address both large-scale water management and microhabitat restoration to buffer against rapid lake-level fluctuations amplified by climate change.

We investigated the effects of beach nourishment on Least Sandpiper (Calidris minutilla) foraging ecology and interspecific interactions across 12 nourished and 12 control beaches along the Mid-Atlantic coast, USA, during autumn migration (2018-2020). Using standardized shorebird surveys, prey availability sampling (sediment cores), and behavioral observations (1,200+ focal samples), we found nourished sites contained 35% lower benthic invertebrate biomass (mean ± SE: 2.1 ± 0.3 g/m² vs. 3.2 ± 0.4 g/m²; t-test: t=3.41, p=0.002) but supported 42% higher sandpiper densities (GLMM: β=0.56, 95% CI 0.21-0.91). Paradoxically, predation risk mediated this pattern: nourished beaches showed 68% fewer avian predators (principally gulls and crows; χ²=14.7, p<0.001), creating predator-free space that increased sandpiper site fidelity despite suboptimal prey conditions. Community analysis (NMDS stress=0.16) revealed significant shifts in shorebird assemblage structure, with nourished beaches dominated by Least Sandpipers (67% of total individuals) versus more even species distributions at control sites. However, recaptures of 23 PIT-tagged juveniles indicated 18% lower mass gain rates at nourished beaches (mixed model: F₁,₈₇=5.2, p=0.02), suggesting potential carryover effects for migrants. Our results demonstrate that coastal engineering can create ecological traps by decoupling habitat selection cues from resource quality, highlighting the need for nourishment designs that incorporate shallow intertidal zones and predator refugia to support migratory shorebirds.

We investigated the impacts of hematozoan parasites on demographic parameters of Dunlin (Calidris alpina arcticola) breeding in the southern Beaufort Sea region of Alaska (70°15'N, 148°30'W) from 2010-2021. Through molecular screening of 2,340 adult and 1,650 juvenile blood samples, we identified two dominant blood parasites: Haemoproteus calidridis (19.4% prevalence, 95% CI 17.8-21.1) and Plasmodium relictum (8.1% prevalence, 95% CI 6.9-9.4). Capture-mark-recapture analysis revealed infected adults exhibited 18% lower annual survival probability (Φ = 0.67 vs 0.82 for uninfected birds; HR = 1.85, p = 0.003) based on Cox proportional hazards models. Nest monitoring showed infected females produced clutches with 12% lower hatching success (β = -0.28 ± 0.11 SE, p = 0.02) and 22% reduced fledging success compared to uninfected counterparts (χ² = 9.34, df=1, p=0.002). Juveniles testing positive for Haemoproteus demonstrated 6% lower first-year survival during southward migration (p = 0.04) based on satellite telemetry data from 127 individuals. However, parasite infection status showed no significant effect on adult breeding site fidelity (p = 0.31) or mate retention rates (p = 0.47). Our longitudinal dataset reveals complex population dynamics where sublethal parasitic infections cumulatively reduce reproductive output and survival probabilities, potentially contributing to the observed 34% decline in this subspecies' abundance since 2000. These findings emphasize the need to incorporate pathogen monitoring into Arctic shorebird conservation strategies, particularly given anticipated climate-mediated shifts in parasite-host dynamics.

This study examined the cumulative effects of oil spills and associated human cleanup activities on Dunlin (Calidris alpina) during wintering periods in the Pacific Northwest (2019-2021). Using satellite telemetry (n=45 individuals) paired with 1,250 behavioral observations, we quantified displacement distances and time-activity budgets before, during, and after three moderate-sized oil spills (15-30 km shoreline impact). Radio-tagged individuals exposed to spills showed 34% reduced foraging efficiency (GLMM: β = -0.41, SE=0.12, p<0.001) and 2.3× higher vigilance rates compared to control sites. Cleanup crews caused acute displacement, with median disturbance distance of 8.2 km (IQR: 5.1-12.4 km) persisting for 4-7 days post-cleanup. However, 62% of displaced birds returned to original sites within two weeks, exhibiting lower site fidelity than non-exposed counterparts (91% retention; χ²=18.3, p<0.001). Chronic oiling reduced subsequent breeding success, with a 18% lower clutch survival rate (n=32 tracked pairs) compared to regional averages. Counterintuitively, individuals with higher mercury loads (12-15 ppm from preening oiled feathers) showed reduced migratory timing precision (r=-0.63, p=0.02), but no significant survival disadvantage over two annual cycles. Results suggest spill mitigation strategies should prioritize timing cleanup activities to avoid peak migration periods while maintaining alternative habitat corridors. Our multi-year tracking reveals both acute behavioral impacts and surprising resilience in this IUCN Near-Threatened species.

We investigated the impacts of traditional egg harvesting on Lesser Yellowlegs (Tringa flavipes) breeding success and coastal habitat utilization across the Yukon-Kuskokwim Delta, Alaska, from 2015-2022. Using a combination of community interviews (n=47 Indigenous harvesters), historical egg harvest records (1950-1985), and nest monitoring of 420 marked pairs, we quantified spatial and temporal changes in harvesting pressure. GPS-tagged adults (n=82) exhibited 30% lower nest site fidelity in areas with intensive egg collection (≥3 eggs/pair/season) compared to protected zones (p=0.014, Cohen's d=0.72). Nest survival probability decreased by 42% when ≥50% of eggs were removed (n=167 nests, logistic exposure model: β=-1.21±0.38 SE, p=0.003). However, habitat loss rates (1.2% annual decline in preferred sedge meadow habitat) showed no direct correlation with localized harvesting activity (R²=0.08, p=0.21), instead being driven primarily by coastal erosion and permafrost thaw (71% of habitat degradation variance explained). Counterintuitively, traditional harvesting areas maintained higher vegetation diversity (Shannon H'=1.8 vs 1.2 in unused areas) due to reduced goose overgrazing. Our findings suggest that while egg collection reduces individual reproductive success (hazard ratio=2.1 for nest abandonment), current harvest levels (<15% of breeding population annually) do not accelerate habitat loss. Adaptive co-management strategies combining Indigenous ecological knowledge with predator-exclusion fencing in critical nesting zones increased fledging success by 65% in pilot communities, demonstrating the viability of culturally informed conservation approaches for this declining shorebird species.

We investigated how declining pH levels in the Yellow Sea's intertidal zones affect juvenile Bar-tailed Godwit (Limosa lapponica baueri) survival during post-breeding migration (2018-2022). Using miniaturized satellite tags (n=120 juveniles) and monthly water chemistry monitoring across 15 mudflats in Jiangsu Province, China, we quantified relationships between carbonate chemistry, prey availability (dominant bivalve Potamocorbula laevis), and first-year survival probabilities. Juvenile godwits arriving at stopover sites with pH <7.95 (n=47) exhibited 32% lower benthic prey intake rates (95% CI: 24-39%) compared to those at pH ≥8.05 (n=73), as measured by combined probe-and-peck counts and fecal DNA metabarcoding. Allometric growth models revealed pH-mediated reductions in daily mass gain (x̄=0.87g/day at pH 7.90 vs 1.42g/day at pH 8.10; p<0.001), with knock-on effects on migration timing. Cox proportional hazards models showed a 22% reduction in annual survival probability (HR=1.52, SE=0.18) associated with each 0.1 pH unit decrease below 8.0. However, interannual variability exceeded pH effects (2018 survival=0.67 vs 2022=0.51), suggesting cumulative impacts from concurrent stressors. Our results indicate ocean acidification is altering critical trophic pathways for juvenile shorebirds, with populations using acidification hotspots (pH <7.92 by 2050 projections) facing recruitment bottlenecks. These findings underscore the need for carbonate chemistry monitoring in coastal habitat conservation plans for migratory shorebirds.

This study investigated the interactive effects of coastal mudflat reclamation and pollution exposure in wintering Purple Sandpipers (Calidris maritima) across 12 sites in the Wadden Sea, Netherlands. Using sediment core analysis (n=360 samples) and blood/tissue sampling (n=84 birds), we compared heavy metal (Pb, Cd, Hg) and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH) concentrations between natural intertidal zones and adjacent reclaimed industrial areas. Birds occupying reclaimed habitats exhibited 38% higher hepatic Pb concentrations (mean±SE: 2.7±0.4 vs. 1.7±0.3 μg/g dw; p=0.012) and 1.8x greater EROD activity (CYP1A biomarker) compared to natural mudflat conspecifics. Stable isotope mixing models revealed reclaimed-area birds derived 62% of their diet from polluted benthic prey versus 29% in natural sites (Bayesian p<0.01). However, no significant differences in renal Cd accumulation or genetic damage (micronucleus assay) were detected between groups. Juveniles showed stronger pollution gradients across habitat types than adults (age×habitat interaction: F₁,₇₈=5.3, p=0.024), with 92% of first-winter birds in reclaimed areas exceeding hepatic Pb toxicity thresholds. Our results demonstrate that habitat modification exacerbates exposure routes for specific contaminants, particularly affecting younger cohorts. These findings highlight the need to integrate coastal development planning with contaminant monitoring, as cumulative stressors may disproportionately impact shorebird populations already facing tidal habitat loss. Conservation strategies should prioritize preserving natural sediment dynamics in critical wintering areas to buffer pollution effects.

We investigated the impacts of accelerating sea-level rise on genetic connectivity and diversity in Snowy Plover (*Charadrius nivosus*) populations along the Gulf of Mexico coastline using a combination of historical museum specimens (n=78, collected 1920-1950) and contemporary samples (n=272, 2015-2022). Microsatellite analysis of 12 polymorphic loci revealed a 30.4% decline in allelic richness (p=0.003) and a 15.7% reduction in observed heterozygosity (p=0.021) in coastal Texas and Louisiana populations, where habitat loss exceeded 68% since 1950. Approximate Bayesian computation indicated a 92% probability that contemporary gene flow rates between major breeding sites have fallen below historical levels (FST increase from 0.12 to 0.18, p<0.001). Landscape genetic models demonstrated that inundation of barrier islands has disrupted previously stable dispersal corridors, with migration probability decreasing by 0.73 per kilometer of lost beach habitat (95% CI: 0.65-0.81). However, four populations in Florida and Tamaulipas maintained high genetic diversity (HE=0.74±0.03), likely facilitated by inland expansion into alternative saline lake habitats. Our results suggest differential vulnerability to coastal squeeze, with northern populations showing 3.2× higher inbreeding coefficients (F=0.14 vs 0.043) compared to southern groups. These findings underscore the need for dynamic conservation strategies that preserve genetic connectivity through both traditional coastal habitats and emerging inland breeding sites while addressing regional disparities in adaptive capacity.

We examined how nutrient enrichment from agricultural runoff influences foraging ecology and habitat selection of Marbled Godwits (Limosa fedoa) across 12 wetland complexes in the Prairie Pothole Region (North Dakota, USA; Saskatchewan, Canada) during breeding seasons (May-July) from 2019-2021. Using GPS telemetry (n=45 adults) combined with weekly invertebrate sampling and water chemistry analysis, we quantified relationships between total nitrogen (TN: 0.8-6.2 mg/L) and phosphorus (TP: 0.05-0.38 mg/L) concentrations and shorebird foraging performance. Godwits in wetlands with elevated TN/TP (>3× reference sites) showed 28% lower prey capture rates (2.1 vs 2.9 items/min, p=0.003) and 19% shallower average probe depths (4.7 vs 5.8 cm, p=0.02), despite 42% higher benthic biomass in enriched sites. Stable isotope analysis (δ¹⁵N, δ¹³C) revealed trophic shifts toward oligochaete worms in polluted wetlands, replacing preferred dipteran larvae. Generalized linear mixed models showed strong avoidance of high-nutrient wetlands during nest site selection (OR=0.32, 95% CI=0.17-0.58), though this did not translate to reduced nest success (78% vs 82% hatch rate). Our results demonstrate nutrient-driven habitat degradation alters prey community composition and foraging efficiency, potentially forcing energy trade-offs that may impact post-breeding survival. These findings underscore the need to address non-point source pollution in shorebird conservation plans, particularly where agricultural intensification intersects with key stopover habitats.

We investigated the impacts of anthropogenic noise pollution on Bar-tailed Godwit (Limosa lapponica baueri) habitat use across 23 coastal sites in the Yellow Sea and Wadden Sea (2018-2022), combining GPS telemetry (n=85 adults), behavioral observations, and acoustic monitoring. Noise levels exceeding 65 dB(A) correlated with 42% reduction in godwit occupancy probability (β=-0.73, SE=0.15, p<0.001), particularly during peak migration periods when birds exhibited heightened sensitivity. Individuals in noisier areas spent 32% less time foraging (mean±SD: 48±6 vs 71±8 min/hr) and showed 27% higher vigilance rates. Coastal zones within 600m of shipping channels experienced 15% faster habitat loss rates compared to quieter areas (0.83 vs 0.98 km²/year loss, p=0.013), mediated through noise-induced avoidance rather than direct habitat destruction. Nighttime noise pollution (55-72 dB(A)) caused disproportionate impacts, reducing roost site fidelity by 58% (95% CI: 43-69%). Our multi-model inference revealed interactive effects where noise exposure amplified habitat loss impacts on body condition (ΔAICc=14.7 vs additive model). These findings demonstrate that auditory stressors indirectly accelerate coastal habitat degradation for shorebirds by rendering otherwise suitable areas functionally unusable. Mitigation measures combining noise-reduction technologies with spatial buffering (≥800m from key intertidal zones) could preserve 23-41% of currently underutilized stopover habitats critical for this declining population.

We investigated population dynamics of Common Sandpipers (Actitis hypoleucos) along a 215-km urbanized river corridor (River Thames, UK) from 2015–2022, analyzing how altered precipitation regimes influence demographic rates. Using mark-recapture data from 15 breeding sites (n=312 adults, 647 juveniles) paired with high-resolution meteorological data, hierarchical Bayesian models revealed precipitation thresholds affecting vital rates. Extreme rainfall events (>75th percentile historical averages) during the breeding season (April–June) reduced nest survival by 22% per 100mm precipitation increase (β = -0.18, SE=0.05), while fledging mass decreased 8% (t=3.1, p=0.002). Conversely, higher winter precipitation in West African wintering grounds (November–February) correlated with 34% greater adult survival (HR=0.66, 95% CI 0.51–0.83). Population matrix models projected 4.2% annual decline under current precipitation trends, but identified critical inflection points where breeding season rainfall exceeding 450mm/month could drive local extirpations within 15 years. Counterintuitively, sites with engineered flood buffers showed 15% lower juvenile recruitment than natural banks (χ²=6.8, p=0.009), suggesting artificial hydrological controls disrupt invertebrate prey phenology. While regional population trajectories varied significantly (λ range 0.87–1.03), drought-prone southern sites demonstrated greater resilience through earlier clutch timing (Δ=9.5 days, F=4.2, p=0.04). Our findings emphasize precipitation-mediated carryover effects across life stages, advocating for integrated flow management spanning temperate breeding and tropical wintering ecosystems to buffer climate impacts on this declining riparian specialist.

We investigated parental care strategies of Wilson's Snipe (Gallinago delicata) in coastal Louisiana marshes following the 2010 Deepwater Horizon oil spill, comparing 15 oil-exposed breeding territories with 22 reference sites from 2015-2018. Using automated radio-telemetry (n=37 adults) and nest cameras (n=112 nests), we quantified incubation patterns, chick provisioning rates, and nest survival. Oil-exposed females showed 28% lower nest attendance (β = -0.34 ± 0.11 SE, p=0.002) and 2.3× higher nest abandonment rates (HR=2.31, 95% CI:1.47-3.62) compared to controls, with abandonment probability positively correlated with sediment polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon concentrations (r=0.63, p<0.001). Male participation did not differ between groups (F₁,₃₅=0.82, p=0.372), suggesting sex-specific vulnerability to contaminant exposure. Nest survival probability declined by 42% in oiled sites (0.61 vs 0.36, ΔAICc=7.2), though chick growth rates remained comparable (t=1.12, p=0.267). Unexpectedly, oil-exposed adults exhibited 15% higher foraging effort (GLMM: χ²=4.91, p=0.027) but lower plasma corticosterone levels (18.7 ± 3.2 ng/mL vs 24.1 ± 4.6 ng/mL, t=2.89, p=0.006), indicating potential endocrine disruption rather than energetic stress. Our results demonstrate multi-year impacts of residual oil on parental investment decisions, with females disproportionately reducing care despite maintained chick provisioning. These sublethal effects highlight the need for habitat prioritization in oil spill response planning, particularly for cryptically nesting shorebirds where contamination may persist in sediments long-term.

We investigated the interactive effects of phenological mismatch and environmental pollution on Peruvian Thick-knees (Burhinus superciliaris) in coastal Lima, Peru, during 2018-2020 breeding seasons. Using GPS telemetry (n = 47 adults) and weekly pollutant sampling from 12 urban wetland sites, we quantified: 1) temporal mismatches between peak prey availability (measured through aquatic invertebrate traps) and nesting initiation dates, and 2) heavy metal (Pb, Cd, Hg) and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH) concentrations in blood samples. Multivariate analyses revealed significant interactions between mismatch severity and pollutant loads (F3,186 = 4.71, p = 0.003), with individuals experiencing >8-day mismatches showing 32% higher blood Pb concentrations (mean ± SE: 2.41 ± 0.18 vs 1.83 ± 0.12 μg/dL) and 27% lower fledging success (χ² = 6.84, p = 0.009) compared to synchronous pairs. PAH metabolites correlated negatively with egg volume (r = -0.51, p = 0.002) but showed no relationship with clutch size. Spatial analyses of GPS fix clusters indicated mismatched birds utilized areas with 43% higher mean PAH deposition rates (Wilcoxon rank-sum test: W = 381, p = 0.017) during chick-rearing. However, hepatic metallothionein levels (n = 23 necropsies) showed no association with mismatch duration (p = 0.21), suggesting compensatory mechanisms for metal detoxification. Our results demonstrate how climate-driven phenological shifts may exacerbate sublethal pollution impacts in urban-adapted shorebirds, highlighting the need for integrated habitat management that addresses both temporal resource matching and spatial contamination gradients.
